Written from Jeremy's laptop session (Claude Code) before moving the work onto the VPS.

on 2026-10-14 between 10:40 and 15:10 UTC.

## Owner decisions made today

10→- **Target is this VPS** (`3tched`, Devuan 6, runit). Not the laptop.

  across reboots until the next release.

  by the base's `/bin`/`/sbin` symlinks and `opt/...` hidden by the `/opt` mount. Layout for a
  root overlay still to be decided.
20→- **op-storage's golden code is not used for releases** (it keeps multiple release versions).
  It is uncommitted (not in the GitHub repo); copies exist only in
  `/srv/git/odbus-btrfs-enforcement-20261013` and the installed daemon, which still serves
  hourly snapshots.
- **Qdrant is part of the release.**
- **EMQX stays in `/opt`** (base system), not in the release.
- **ZeroClaw → `threetched`**: install upstream ZeroClaw, rename the binary to `threetched`.
  **No patches** — `vendor/tched-router/patches/*` are deprecated (our code is separated from
  upstream; it should be plain upgrades). The patches may have caused earlier bugs.
  Config directory goes in `/opt` and is the only place that keeps the ZeroClaw name
30→  (proposed `/opt/zeroclaw`; upstream reads `ZEROCLAW_CONFIG_DIR`). Old config exists at
  `/home/jeremy/.zeroclaw` (Aug, 588K).
- The repo will be **pulled**, not copied from the laptop.

## Findings

1. **Hourly snapshots stalled since 2026-10-14 02:00Z.** That run published set
   `4883943c-142e-481b-9b09-09440684db43` (all 7 members), then the hourly cleanup of the previous set
   deleted the old `home` snapshot and got `EPERM` on `logs` (subvolume 270). `pending.json`
   (phase `retiring_previous_host_set`) now blocks every run ("Prior run is incomplete").
40→   op-storage *is* in the trusted guard cgroup (`/opdbus-storage`, id 6364, both FSIDs), has
   full caps, no file attributes, no default-subvolume involvement. Leading hypothesis: a
   concurrent `btrfs send` of that snapshot (kernel returns EPERM for delete-during-send);
   not proven. The guard did deny 212 native btrfs ioctls from untrusted callers (counter 0).
2. **Ownership change at 07:48Z** (owner did it deliberately, now says put it back):

   for its destinations: `/opt`, `/opt/op-dbus`, `/opt/op-dbus/system-snapshots/*`,
   `/opt/op-dbus/send`, `/opt/op-dbus/vector-store` (+`timing`, `vectors`, `.writer.lock`),
   `/opt/op-dbus/vector-captures`, `/opt/op-dbus/development-checkpoints`.
50→   The 02:00Z snapshot set holds the pre-chown owners/modes. A read-only comparison ran at
   14:57Z; per-member lists are in `/root/ownership-restore-20261014/` (`*.restore.tsv` =
   back to 02:00Z owner/mode, `*.new.tsv` = created after 02:00Z, no record). Restore counts:
   `/` 1, `/opt` 33, `/home` 5, `/var/log` 71, `/srv/git` 4,367, cargo-build 20,935, golden 1.
   Nothing has been changed yet.
3. **Old system content copied into `/opt` at 06:05:26Z** (after the 02:00Z snapshot): the fresh
   `/opt` held only `nodejs` and `op-dbus` (root-owned). Added: antigravity-ide, audit, btmp,
   claude-code, critical, emqx (link), emqx-6.2.2, emqx-6.2.2-c5b549…, google,
   google-cloud-cli, Grok Bot, oci-cli, op-mcp-providers, opdbus, opt, pacman.log, telnet,
   wtmp, Zenflow (~5.8 GB). Sources exist on the recovery disk (`p3-btrfs/@/opt`,
60→   `vdb-p2/@/opt`). Owner keeps EMQX; the rest is undecided.
4. **EMQX**: the system uses `emqx-6.2.2-c5b549d312d…` (version + SHA-256 pin in
   `deploy/config/emqx.version`). `emqx-6.2.2` is a byte-identical duplicate. `/opt/emqx`
   currently points at nonexistent `/opt/op-dbus/current/opt/emqx`. Both copies' `etc` →
   `/etc/emqx`, which does not exist; user `emqx` and an `emqx` runit service do not exist.
5. **threetched build**: a patched build was started then stopped at owner's direction; no
   processes remain. Leftovers: partial cache `/var/lib/cargo-build/threetched-cache`, empty
   `/var/lib/cargo-build/odbus-verified/threetched-artifacts/tched-router`.

   101 on missing threetched input). `mdadm` runit service flaps (enabled, `/etc/sv/mdadm`
70→   missing). `/opt/op-dbus/current` → nonexistent `releases/…-e46dad8`. No network topology
   (only eth0): no OVS/WG/Xray/WARP/incus. Two Qdrant instances: 6343 (runit
   `qdrant-drive-recovered`, `/mnt/qdrant-drive-recovery`, 26 collections, verified docs
   round-trip, full snapshot sha `bce23c66…`) and 6335 (manual, root, recovery-disk
   `overlay-work/qdrant-run`, go/python/c/java/docs + 430k rust_lang_rust).
   Reboot validation still outstanding.

## Voice over SSH (set up today)

`vps-voice` on the laptop reverse-forwards the laptop's PipeWire-Pulse socket to
80→`~/.pulse-laptop/native` on the VPS. Installed `libasound2-plugins libsox-fmt-pulse
pulseaudio-utils`; `~/.asoundrc` (ALSA default → pulse) and `~/.config/pulse/client.conf`
for root and jeremy (originals backed up as `*.before-voice-20261014` if present — none were).
Verified `arecord`/`rec` capture the laptop mic. `xcb_connection_has_error` noise comes from
`DISPLAY=:20` in jeremy's rc files; harmless, or start with `DISPLAY= claude`.

- Ownership restore scope (everything vs `/opt` + storage paths) — then finish the
  interrupted hourly cleanup and clear `pending.json`.
90→- Remaining old `/opt` content: remove or keep.
- Golden layout for a root overlay; where Qdrant live data lives (read-only release layer).
- Which Qdrant data set becomes the release copy (6343, 6335, or merge).
- ZeroClaw upstream version to install (pin was v0.8.4, commit a56c345d…).

## Update 15:25Z — hourly snapshots unblocked by hand; permanent fix still needed

- Ownership put back to `root:root` (modes unchanged) on the 18 paths op-storage manages:
  `/opt`, `/opt/op-dbus`, `golden`, `send`, `development-checkpoints`, `vector-captures`
  (+ `capture-616299d0…`), `vector-store` (+ `.writer.lock`, `timing`, `vectors`),
100→  `system-snapshots` + its 6 member dirs. Before-state:
  `/root/ownership-restore-20261014/by-hand-before-20261014T151218Z.tsv`. Everything else
  left as is (cleanup later, per owner).
- Interrupted cleanup finished by hand (6 calls); only set `4883943c` remains (all 7 members);
  `pending.json` cleared; `last.json` marks "manual reconciliation" at 15:13:44Z.
- **Root cause:** op-storage `delete_by_id` (`crates/op-storage/src/engine.rs`, NativeBackend)
  calls `btrfs_uapi::subvolume::subvol_sync_wait_one` after each `subvolume_delete_by_id`.
  That is `BTRFS_IOC_SUBVOL_SYNC_WAIT` (ioctl 65). Kernel 6.12.111 does not implement it
  (UAPI header stops at 64; nothing in kallsyms), and the guard denies the unknown encoding
  even for the trusted cgroup → EPERM. The delete itself succeeds, so every call removed one
110→  member and then failed. Guard counters confirmed one denial per deletion.
- **Next hourly run (16:00Z) will stall again** after deleting one old member.
- **Fix (owner said "whatever you think is right"):** remove the `subvol_sync_wait_one` call
  from `delete_by_id` in the VPS source `/srv/git/odbus-btrfs-enforcement-20261013/crates/op-storage`
  (the running binary 4039cec2… was built from it; the laptop copy is older — ignore it).
  The existing readback (`child(...).is_none()`) already verifies removal. Then rebuild,
  install to `/usr/local/libexec/opdbus-storage/op-storage`, update its line in
  `manifest.sha256` (bootstrap check verifies all 7 hashes), `sv restart op-storage`, and
  run `/usr/local/libexec/opdbus-storage/op-storage-hourly` once to prove a full cycle.
  Allowing ioctl 65 in the guard would not help on this kernel.
120→
## Kernel plan (owner, 15:30Z)

Owner will upgrade to the **XanMod** kernel first, then fix hourly cleanup. Consequences:
`/usr/local/libexec/opdbus-storage/bootstrap-check.sh` pins `uname -r` = `6.12.111+deb13-amd64` and
the BTF sha256, so the guard service (and op-storage behind it) will refuse to start on the new
kernel until the guard is rebuilt (`/root/btrfs-enforcement-20261013/kernel-guard/build.sh`
regenerates the allowlist from the new UAPI/BTF), the pins and `manifest.sha256` are updated, and
the guard is reloaded (stop op-storage, `guardctl mode off`, `guardctl unload`, start guard service).
BPF LSM must be enabled on the new kernel (`lsm=` includes `bpf`). The GRUB/BIOS boot repair has
130→never been reboot-tested — keep console access ready. If the new kernel has
`BTRFS_IOC_SUBVOL_SYNC_WAIT` (ioctl 65), add it to `known_management` in `generate-allow.c`;
otherwise remove `subvol_sync_wait_one` from op-storage `delete_by_id`.

**Owner requirement:** kernel upgrades must not break the system. The exact `uname -r` + BTF-hash
pin makes every upgrade disable the guard and op-storage until a manual rebuild; that has to change
(e.g. regenerate/verify the allowlist automatically from the installed UAPI during kernel install,
keeping the object CO-RE portable) so a XanMod upgrade boots with storage working.

140→
Owner: "the network needs to be part of the golden" — chicken-and-egg: deploying/repairing a
release needs network access, but the network itself ships in the release. Suggested resolution to
discuss: the base system keeps a minimal management path that never depends on a release (eth0 +
SSH, console as last resort); the release carries the 3tched topology (OVS, Xray/REALITY, WARP,
private 10.0.0.x, decoy path). A release that breaks networking is recovered by booting the previous
slot or `opdbus.overlay=off`. Not decided.

Owner follow-up: **build the network directly into the golden subvolume** (`/opt/op-dbus/golden`).
It is not live until a slot is activated at boot, so base `eth0` + SSH keeps access during the
150→build. Requires golden to be root-shaped (network files at real paths: `etc/sv/…`, `etc/xray/…`,
`etc/network/interfaces.d/…`), and the base must not hold competing network files (base wins on
conflicts) — keep only the management path there; decide NetworkManager's role.

## Update 17:20Z — release slots staged (Claude, not installed)

Owner: ~72 releases/day → live swap, active re-mounted at boot; overlay on a release-owned
path (`/opt/op-dbus/current`), not `/`; network stays on the base system with a preinstall
script (supersedes the 15:35Z "network in golden" note); a separate guard-trusted cgroup like
op-storage for golden releases. Kit, README and install/rollback scripts:
160→`/root/btrfs-enforcement-20261013/deployment-release-slots-20261014/`. Source:
`/srv/git/odbus-btrfs-enforcement-20261013/crates/op-storage/src/bin/op-release.rs`
(+ `receive_generated` made `pub` in golden.rs). Built, never run. Nothing on the host changed.
Cargo dispatcher needs `CARGO_REAL_BINARY` and the rustup toolchain on PATH (no /usr/bin/cargo).

Installed (owner-approved): release kit (empty slots @release-a/@release-b on root fs), `@incus`
on sda2 at /var/lib/incus/disks (fstab, no `nofail`!), Incus 6.0.4 with one btrfs pool `3tched`
(loop image, fsid a1ab7b42…), guard trusts cgroup opdbus-incus for that fsid only. Deleted the
78 GB vdb recovery images in ~jeremy; space held by hourly set e5c37c9a home snapshot (subvol 283).
170→Owner is booting recovery to repartition sda2 for a vector partition and delete files. Owner wants
no retirement code and every Btrfs issue fixed before continuing. After offline changes, reconcile
op-storage state.json, hourly/pending.json and storage-policy.json pins before it runs again.
Snowball decision: ledger only, vectors decoupled, no "timing" naming in snowball, no timing rotation.

## Update 23:40Z — LVM + guard UUIDs (Claude, from live CD chroot)
- New VG 3tched-vg spans sdb1, sdb2, sdc5. LVs: root (d53eeac0), swap, cargo 1.39T (328bc09f =
  the former RECOVERY fs, now also holds a new @cargo-build), vectors 32G (3b3fd476),
  ct-upgrade 20G (0d7e3795), seed 20G (e9cf9d60, Ubuntu 26.04 root, NOT yet SEEDING).
- sda2 (083161be) NOT migrated: @opt @git @logs @cargo-build @golden @incus @home still there and
180→  in fstab. Owner wants /home moved to the OS (root) LV.
- Guard: op-storage cgroup now also trusted for vectors, ct-upgrade, cargo (bootstrap-check.sh
  STORAGE_FSID_VECTORS/UPGRADE/CARGO, guard run trust lines, ready check). Seed: no trust (RO).
  Manifest rebuilt (11). Backups: /root/btrfs-enforcement-20261013/deployment-release-slots-20261014/
  before-lvm-uuids-20261014T233056Z/. Untested until boot (live kernel ≠ pinned 6.12.111).
- fstab /srv/seed pointed at nonexistent ec66acdf → fixed to e9cf9d60.
- Seed: OS moved into @ (snapshot of top level, originals removed); seed fstab root subvol=@.
  No GRUB from the Ubuntu install (no i386-pc, install_devices empty).
- ct-upgrade: empty @ created (empty `data` subvolume left in place).
- Deferred to the installed system (no double chroot): seed services from
190→  deploy/workspace-image (3tchedfs.service, preflight, prepare-lungs-client.sh) need a built
  threetched-fs + sealed catalog; lungs socket is host-provided per design (owner to confirm);
  networkmanager-rs source missing (empty dir in all checkouts). Then set the seed flag.
- op-storage hard-codes RECOVERY_FS=328bc09f (now the cargo LV) — check before it manages cargo.

## Update 2026-10-15 — storage reshuffle, home move, delete fix (Claude, live CD chroot)

Owner decisions:
- sda (640G) is in `3tched-vg` (PVs: sda2, sdc5). The 1.5T sdb was only for recovery and is being trashed: all of its LVs go, including cargo (and the Qdrant 6335 data on it).
- `/home` is the `@home` subvolume on the root fs (d53eeac0). It is still its own subvolume.
200→- Vectors are a log of the runtime env, a **hash chain**. They are never in the release stream and never in hourly snapshots. They live in persistent RW storage outside releases and are never restored from a snapshot.

#
# Location: ~/.config/voxtype/config.toml
# All settings can be overridden via CLI flags

# State file for external integrations (Waybar, polybar, etc.)
# Use "auto" for default location ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/voxtype/state),
# a custom path, or "disabled" to turn off. The daemon writes state
# ("idle", "recording", "transcribing") to this file whenever it changes.

state_file = "auto"

[hotkey]
# Key to hold for push-to-talk
# Common choices: SCROLLLOCK, PAUSE, RIGHTALT, F13-F24
# Use `evtest` to find key names for your keyboard
key = "SCROLLLOCK"

# Optional modifier keys that must also be held
20→# Example: modifiers = ["LEFTCTRL", "LEFTALT"]
modifiers = []

# Activation mode: "push_to_talk" or "toggle"
# - push_to_talk: Hold hotkey to record, release to transcribe (default)
# - toggle: Press hotkey once to start recording, press again to stop
# mode = "push_to_talk"

# Set to false when using compositor keybindings (Hyprland, Sway) instead
30→# When disabled, use `voxtype record start/stop/toggle` to control recording

# Modifier key to select secondary model (evdev input mode only)
# When held while pressing the hotkey, uses whisper.secondary_model instead
# Example: model_modifier = "LEFTSHIFT"  # Shift+hotkey uses secondary model

[audio]

All captures are zero duration. This is a parecord tunnel issue, not just a mute problem.

The first capture yielded 0.37 seconds of silence. Later attempts return empty frames. Parecord may not flush on SIGINT over this PulseAudio version, or the connection breaks after the first recording. I will test pactl, pw-record, and ffmpeg to verify the connection. I also plan to try raw parec output with a byte limit.

I will check the system journal for PulseAudio errors. The SSH tunnel may be stuck after the first connection, though pactl and the initial capture both succeeded.

Parecord likely writes its WAV header only when the process closes cleanly, so SIGINT or timeout leaves the file empty. The first capture was short because the default SIGTERM timed out early. I will switch to `parec` with raw output and use `dd` or `timeout` to measure actual bytes, bypassing the header flush problem.

The PulseAudio server might reject the connection due to a cookie or a suspended source. The USB microphone may also need more than two seconds to wake up.

I will check `pactl list source-outputs` during recording and run `parec` in the background to measure bytes before killing it.

Voxtype likely reports no audio because the device was muted, causing exact silence. Unmuting may be the real fix, while the parecord tests are just a measurement problem.

The "No audio was captured" warning likely means the recorder failed to open the device or received zero frames, not just silence. If the USB microphone is muted, PipeWire may deliver only zeros, which voxtype VAD would reject. Whisper could still hallucinate on that silent input.

I will unmute the default USB microphone and capture raw audio to verify it is producing sound. I will measure peak and RMS levels from that capture. If the source still yields no data, I will test other available sources. I will also run a short voxtype recording to check the logs.

content.text:
The source went idle after being woken. Parecord wrote zero bytes.

The first parecord captured 64KB before stopping. The server briefly accepted a client connection. The zero-byte file suggests parecord opened the socket but hung before writing samples. This points to an SSH unix socket forwarding bug or a protocol hang.

A cookie mismatch is unlikely because pactl works. The next step is to strace parecord for two seconds to see what it is doing. This appears to be a known OpenSSH Unix socket forwarding issue with PulseAudio.

Native PulseAudio over SSH is a known working pattern. The zero-byte file may be caused by a hard kill interrupting parecord before it flushed its buffer.

I will test ffmpeg and sox capture next. I also plan to verify playback with paplay to confirm the tunnel carries audio both ways.

rawOutput.description: Debug why Pulse capture writes no samples

content.text:
This is a classic PulseAudio over SSH problem.

The client advances time but never receives audio data. The server buffer fills while the client reads nothing. PulseAudio uses shared memory by default, which breaks over SSH.

The fix is to disable shared memory in `~/.config/pulse/client.conf` by setting `enable-shm = no`. This forces PulseAudio to send audio inline over the SSH socket instead of using shared memory file descriptors.

The current `client.conf` lacks `enable-shm = no`. Adding it should fix parec, sox, and the voxtype daemon. The running voxtype daemon may not need a restart if libpulse reads the configuration at connection time.

Restarting the voxtype daemon is the safest way to ensure it picks up the new `enable-shm = no` setting. PipeWire's Pulse compatibility layer also respects this client.conf flag.

A temporary test can use `PULSE_CLIENTCONFIG=/tmp/client.conf` to verify the fix without editing the permanent file. Cookie authentication is already working. The `default-server` setting should remain in `client.conf` alongside `enable-shm = no`.

The server-side pipewire likely needs no changes. The client setting alone should force inline audio over the socket.

I will update client.conf and test capture RMS before testing voxtype. I also need to check root's configuration since both sides were configured.

The voxtype daemon is started by hyprland autostart, not a systemd service. Killing it will not cause an automatic respawn.

I will test parecord first to verify the fix without restarting the daemon. If voxtype still fails, I will restart it with the same command. I also need to check `client.conf.before-vpn-audio`. The missing `enable-shm = no` is exactly why voxtype captured nothing over SSH.

I'll add `enable-shm = no` and test.

Pulse plugin should honor `enable-shm`. Some pipewire versions still use memfd despite that flag. `PIPEWIRE_REMOTE` won't work across SSH. I'll update the config and test parecord first. Then I'll test voxtype.

The voxtype daemon likely cached the old audio backend. I'll kill it and restart it to apply the config change.

I'll check root's client.conf with sudo. I'll add a comment to match the file style and clean up /tmp wav files after testing. I'm also checking whether voxtype VAD might falsely trigger on ambient room noise.

The microphone was previously muted. Unmuting it and disabling shared memory should restore audio. A zero RMS reading would indicate a hardware failure or persistent mute state. The device is still connected, so the issue is likely software-related.

A known pipewire-pulse bug ignores `enable-shm=no` and still uses memfd. This matches the symptom exactly: latency climbs forever with no samples written. If that flag fails, loading a native TCP protocol module on the laptop is not viable because the SSH tunnel only forwards Unix sockets.

A userspace proxy on the VPS would not help because it still requires shared memory. Recent PipeWire versions do honor `enable-shm = no`, so the latency symptom confirms the flag is being ignored. The environment variable `PULSE_SHM=0` does not exist; only the config key works. I will also try setting `pulse.allow-shm = false` via `pactl` on the laptop.

The SSH tunnel reaches the laptop, but Pulse is handing audio through shared memory, which cannot cross SSH. Voxtype therefore records silence. I'll turn shared memory off and confirm the mic actually arrives.

I will run `PULSE_LOG=4 parec` to verify client.conf is read. The `enable-shm = no` syntax is standard and should be parsed correctly.

content.text:
Shared memory is not possible.

Memfd is possible and private SHM was negotiated. PipeWire may still be using memfd despite the disabled classic POSIX SHM. Data is still not arriving.

This is a known PipeWire issue. The server may still be writing to memfd and sending the descriptor via SCM_RIGHTS. SSHD forwarding might pass those descriptors through.

OpenSSH stream local forwarding does not forward file descriptors. The memfd descriptor would be invalid on the remote side. The log wording is confusing: "Negotiated SHM: no" likely refers only to POSIX SHM, while private memfd may still be active.

"Private" likely means PA_MEM_TYPE_PRIVATE, which copies data into private memory from the socket. That would be correct for network transport. The server is still not sending audio blocks. It only sends timing updates, so latency keeps increasing.

The sshd process on the laptop can receive memfd descriptors locally, but it does not forward them to the remote TCP channel. This explains why the client reports no shared memory while audio data still fails to arrive.

The VPS sshd listens on the local Pulse socket and forwards raw bytes over the SSH channel. PipeWire sends memfd descriptors to the local ssh process, which never forwards them to the remote side. The client likely expects inline data because it reports no shared memory, but PipeWire may still be emitting memfd blocks anyway.

The fix is to disable memfd and shared memory on the laptop PipeWire server. I am checking PipeWire pulse module options such as `pulse.allow-shm` and `pulse.properties` to find a remote configuration method.

I found a workaround in a PipeWire GitLab issue. The fix involves adding `pulse.properties` to the protocol-pulse module arguments in `~/.config/pipewire/pipewire-pulse.conf`. I am also checking whether an environment variable like `PIPEWIRE_PULSE_DISABLE_SHM` can disable shared memory remotely.

The laptop runs PipeWire 1.6.9, a very recent release. This raises the possibility of a regression causing silence for remote clients. Earlier strace output confirms that only small control messages arrive over the socket, with no audio data packets detected.

Audio fragments are roughly 64000 bytes, confirming the server is not sending audio payloads. The client received a connection acknowledgment but no data messages. The source may be suspended or muted, though that would not explain why latency keeps climbing as if buffered data were arriving.

Latency equals elapsed time. The client read index is frozen because no audio data arrives. The server write index advances because it thinks it is buffering. This confirms a shared memory desync: PipeWire is writing to memfd while the remote client cannot read it. The client log claiming "Negotiated SHM: no" likely precedes the server forcing memfd, or the "private" type label is misleading.

I need to read the full pulse log file rather than just the filtered output. I am checking whether `pactl` can change server properties, since `pw-cli` and `pw-metadata` connect to the local PipeWire socket while the SSH tunnel only forwards the Pulse socket.

I considered using `pactl` to load a TCP protocol module on the laptop, but that would require a new tunnel and is impractical. A Pulse proxy would not fix the server-side shared memory issue either.

content.text:
The memblockq sanitized output looks interesting.

The memblockq parameters were sanitized unexpectedly. minreq jumped from 0 to 2 bytes, while tlength grew to 4 MB. base=2 and prebuf=2 also appeared. This is far below the expected values.

A known PipeWire bug likely causes the corruption. The SSH socket appears local to libpulse because it is a Unix domain socket, so "Is Local" reads yes over SSH. This triggers incorrect buffer negotiation and tiny byte sizes.

PipeWire treats the SSH client as local because it connects through a Unix socket. It sends audio via memfd file descriptors. The SSH process drops those descriptors. The VPS pulse client never receives the data. PipeWire expects inline data instead, but the client has no SHM support.

PipeWire likely ignores the client's SHM flag for Unix socket connections and always uses memfd. This matches issue #1840 in the PipeWire tracker.

The client reports a normal fragsize of 64000 bytes, so the tiny minreq=2 is a parsing bug over the connection. The server should send 64 KB blocks, but they are not arriving.

I will fetch the PipeWire pulse-server source to see how it sends record data.

A workaround is to use the PulseAudio TCP module or socat. The enable-shm=no setting works for PulseAudio but not PipeWire.

For PipeWire, a protocol-pulse listener that disables memfd may be needed. I am checking pipewire-pulse.conf.d for relevant properties.

content.text:
Audio is arriving. It is 2 seconds long with a peak of 1382 and an RMS of 194.

The earlier zero-byte files happened because the capture stopped before the 64000-byte fragment could flush. The tunnel works once the full fragment arrives. Voxtype failed after only 0.6 seconds with "No audio was captured".

The microphone was muted when voxtype started. Its ALSA plugin likely requested a smaller buffer than PipeWire's 2-second default capture size, causing it to time out before the first fragment arrived.

The server clamps client buffer requests to a minimum of 5.3 ms, but it still waits two seconds before delivering the first chunk. A 0.6-second capture therefore receives nothing, which explains the "No audio was captured" error. The fix must account for this two-second latency on the SSH link.

Shared memory is already disabled, so data crosses the SSH tunnel. The 64 KB chunk confirms this works.

The two-second default fragment is the real problem. Voxtype needs smaller fragments to avoid missing audio on short recordings.

I am checking whether parecord's `--latency-msec` or `--process-time-msec` flags can request a smaller buffer from the server. The 64000-byte result might have come from parecord's own default rather than the server clamping up.

I will test parecord with `--latency-msec=50` or `--process-time-msec=20` to see if the server honors a smaller client buffer. The voxtype error "No audio was captured" likely means zero samples were received, not just silence being rejected by voice activity detection.

VAD is commented out, so the default is off.

The "no audio" message likely comes from a zero-sample or zero-RMS check. The microphone is now unmuted and producing RMS values of 24–194, so samples should be captured. An energy gate may still be active even though VAD is off; the config shows an external trigger threshold of -20 dBFS.

RMS 24 equals roughly -62 dBFS, well below the -20 dBFS threshold. The test failed because the microphone was muted and produced exact zeros. A 2.5-second voxtype recording will reveal whether the pipeline works or if ALSA fragment size and pulse plugin latency need adjustment.

The ALSA pulse plugin uses default buffer attributes, so the 2-second Pipewire fragment is likely in effect. A 3-second voxtype test will be run to check the daemon log. The daemon does not need a restart because libpulse is already initialized.

The daemon likely cached the libpulse context from its first connection, so it still uses the old shared-memory setting. The earlier "no audio" error may have been caused by that stale configuration rather than a mute. A restart is required to pick up the new `enable-shm=no` setting.

The entire process chain will be killed and restarted to avoid duplicate daemons. The test will use `voxtype record start`, sleep for three seconds, then `voxtype record stop`.

The error message contains avg_rms and threshold values, suggesting an energy gate check runs before the failure. The daemon log currently shows INFO level output, so a DEBUG log level will be needed to see those intermediate metrics.

I will check the voxtype source code on disk to see how it handles quiet recordings. I also need to configure low latency in asoundrc or the Pulse client so short dictation works. The cpal ALSA "default" device might not inherit the Pulse client.conf shared-memory setting.

The libpulse client.conf only controls connection and shared-memory settings; fragment size is set by the application. The user's mention of "each" likely means both the jeremy and root accounts need configuration.

The phrase "iscahn use3 voxstypse3" likely means "I can use voxtype." I will check root's client.conf next. The microphone stays unmuted. The 4-second capture with shared-memory disabled produced real audio, so the earlier zero-sample failure was caused by the microphone being muted. The latency climb symptom is classic shared-memory behavior.

The 4-second capture returned exactly one fragment of real audio, confirming the shared-memory fix works. The low latency test captured 0.3 seconds in one second.

The voxtype daemon was restarted with that config. A 2.5 second recording captured 1.6 seconds of audio and Whisper ran. The transcript was empty because the room was quiet.

Scroll Lock, or the remote Ctrl+Alt+V binding, toggles dictation. Speak after you start it, then press the key again to transcribe.

# Whisper

## Overview

Transcribe audio with OpenAI's Whisper — the state-of-the-art speech recognition model. This skill covers local Whisper (Python), faster-whisper (CTranslate2, 4x faster), whisper.cpp (CPU-optimized C++), and the OpenAI Whisper API. Includes subtitle generation (SRT/VTT/JSON), multi-language transcription, translation to English, speaker diarization, word-level timestamps, and production pipeline patterns for podcasts, meetings, and video subtitles.
30→
## Instructions

### Step 1: Choose Your Runtime

**Option A — OpenAI Whisper (original Python):**
```bash
pip install openai-whisper
# Models: tiny (39M), base (74M), small (244M), medium (769M), large-v3 (1.5G)
```
40→
**Option B — faster-whisper (recommended for local, 4x faster):**
```bash
pip install faster-whisper
# Uses CTranslate2 — INT8 quantization, runs well on CPU
```

**Option C — whisper.cpp (best for CPU, minimal dependencies):**
```bash
git clone https://github.com/ggerganov/whisper.cpp
50→cd whisper.cpp && make
# Download model
bash models/download-ggml-model.sh base.en
```

**Option D — OpenAI API (no local GPU needed):**
```bash
pip install openai
export OPENAI_API_KEY=***

```
60→
### Step 2: Basic Transcription

**faster-whisper (recommended):**
```python
from faster_whisper import WhisperModel

model = WhisperModel("base", device="cpu", compute_type="int8")
# GPU: model = WhisperModel("large-v3", device="cuda", compute_type="float16")

70→segments, info = model.transcribe("episode.mp3", beam_size=5)
print(f"Language: {info.language} (prob: {info.language_probability:.2f})")

for segment in segments:
    print(f"[{segment.start:.2f}s → {segment.end:.2f}s] {segment.text}")
```

**OpenAI Whisper (original):**
```python
import whisper
80→
model = whisper.load_model("base")  # tiny, base, small, medium, large-v3
result = model.transcribe("episode.mp3")

print(result["text"])
for segment in result["segments"]:
    print(f"[{segment['start']:.1f}s - {segment['end']:.1f}s] {segment['text']}")
```

**whisper.cpp (CLI):**
90→```bash
./main -m models/ggml-base.en.bin -f episode.wav -otxt -osrt -ovtt
# Outputs: episode.txt, episode.srt, episode.vtt
```

**OpenAI API:**
```python
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()

100→with open("episode.mp3", "rb") as f:
    transcript = client.audio.transcriptions.create(
        model="whisper-1",
        file=f,
        response_format="verbose_json",
        timestamp_granularities=["segment", "word"],
    )

print(transcript.text)
for segment in transcript.segments:
110→    print(f"[{segment.start:.1f}s] {segment.text}")
```

### Step 3: Subtitle Generation (SRT/VTT)

**Generate SRT with faster-whisper:**
```python
from faster_whisper import WhisperModel

model = WhisperModel("small", device="cpu", compute_type="int8")
120→segments, info = model.transcribe("episode.mp3", beam_size=5)

def format_timestamp(seconds):
    h = int(seconds // 3600)
    m = int((seconds % 3600) // 60)
    s = int(seconds % 60)
    ms = int((seconds % 1) * 1000)
    return f"{h:02d}:{m:02d}:{s:02d},{ms:03d}"

with open("episode.srt", "w") as f:
130→    for i, seg in enumerate(segments, 1):
        f.write(f"{i}\n")
        f.write(f"{format_timestamp(seg.start)} --> {format_timestamp(seg.end)}\n")
        f.write(f"{seg.text.strip()}\n\n")

print("Generated episode.srt")
```

**Generate VTT (for HTML5 video):**
```python
140→with open("episode.vtt", "w") as f:
    f.write("WEBVTT\n\n")
    for i, seg in enumerate(segments, 1):
        start = format_timestamp(seg.start).replace(",", ".")
        end = format_timestamp(seg.end).replace(",", ".")
        f.write(f"{start} --> {end}\n")
        f.write(f"{seg.text.strip()}\n\n")
```

**Word-level timestamps (for karaoke-style subtitles):**
150→```python
segments, info = model.transcribe("episode.mp3", word_timestamps=True)
for segment in segments:
    for word in segment.words:
        print(f"  [{word.start:.2f}s → {word.end:.2f}s] {word.word}")
```

### Step 4: Language Detection & Translation

```python
160→# Auto-detect language
segments, info = model.transcribe("foreign_audio.mp3")
print(f"Detected: {info.language} ({info.language_probability:.0%})")

# Force specific language
segments, info = model.transcribe("german.mp3", language="de")

# Translate to English (any language → English)
segments, info = model.transcribe("german.mp3", task="translate")
for seg in segments:
170→    print(seg.text)  # English translation
```

**Supported languages:** 99 languages including en, zh, de, es, ru, ko, fr, ja, pt, tr, pl, nl, ar, sv, it, hi, and many more.

### Step 5: Speaker Diarization

Combine Whisper with pyannote-audio for "who said what":

```python
180→from faster_whisper import WhisperModel
from pyannote.audio import Pipeline
import torch

# Transcribe
model = WhisperModel("small", device="cpu", compute_type="int8")
segments, info = model.transcribe("meeting.wav", beam_size=5)
whisper_segments = list(segments)

# Diarize (requires HuggingFace token with pyannote access)
190→diarization = Pipeline.from_pretrained(
    "pyannote/speaker-diarization-3.1",
    use_auth_token=***

)
diarization_result = diarization("meeting.wav")

# Merge: assign speaker to each whisper segment
def get_speaker(start, end, diarization_result):
    """Find the dominant speaker during a time range."""
    speakers = {}
200→    for turn, _, speaker in diarization_result.itertracks(yield_label=True):
        overlap_start = max(start, turn.start)
        overlap_end = min(end, turn.end)
        if overlap_start < overlap_end:
            duration = overlap_end - overlap_start
            speakers[speaker] = speakers.get(speaker, 0) + duration
    return max(speakers, key=speakers.get) if speakers else "Unknown"

for seg in whisper_segments:
    speaker = get_speaker(seg.start, seg.end, diarization_result)
210→    print(f"[{speaker}] [{seg.start:.1f}s → {seg.end:.1f}s] {seg.text}")
```

### Step 6: Batch Processing & Pipelines

**Transcribe all episodes in a directory:**
```python
import os
from pathlib import Path
from faster_whisper import WhisperModel
220→
model = WhisperModel("small", device="cpu", compute_type="int8")
episodes_dir = Path("episodes")
output_dir = Path("transcripts")
output_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

for audio_file in sorted(episodes_dir.glob("*.mp3")):
    print(f"Transcribing: {audio_file.name}")
    segments, info = model.transcribe(str(audio_file), beam_size=5)
    
230→    # Plain text
    txt_path = output_dir / f"{audio_file.stem}.txt"
    with open(txt_path, "w") as f:
        for seg in segments:
            f.write(seg.text.strip() + "\n")
    
    # SRT
    srt_path = output_dir / f"{audio_file.stem}.srt"
    segments2, _ = model.transcribe(str(audio_file), beam_size=5)  # Re-iterate
    with open(srt_path, "w") as f:
240→        for i, seg in enumerate(segments2, 1):
            h, m = divmod(int(seg.start), 3600)
            m, s = divmod(m, 60)
            ms = int((seg.start % 1) * 1000)
            start_ts = f"{h:02d}:{m:02d}:{s:02d},{ms:03d}"
            h2, m2 = divmod(int(seg.end), 3600)
            m2, s2 = divmod(m2, 60)
            ms2 = int((seg.end % 1) * 1000)
            end_ts = f"{h2:02d}:{m2:02d}:{s2:02d},{ms2:03d}"
            f.write(f"{i}\n{start_ts} --> {end_ts}\n{seg.text.strip()}\n\n")
250→    
    print(f"  → {txt_path}, {srt_path}")
```

### Step 7: Model Selection Guide

| Model | Size | VRAM | Speed (CPU) | Accuracy | Best For |
|-------|------|------|-------------|----------|----------|
| tiny | 39M | ~1GB | Very fast | Low | Quick drafts, real-time |
| base | 74M | ~1GB | Fast | Medium | Good balance for CPU |
260→| small | 244M | ~2GB | Moderate | Good | Podcasts, clear audio |
| medium | 769M | ~5GB | Slow | Very good | Noisy audio, accents |
| large-v3 | 1.5G | ~10GB | Very slow | Best | Production quality |

**Recommendations:**
- CPU-only, speed matters: `tiny` or `base` with faster-whisper
- CPU-only, accuracy matters: `small` with faster-whisper
- GPU available: `large-v3` with faster-whisper (`float16`)
- No local compute: OpenAI API (`whisper-1`)

270→## Examples

### Example 1: Transcribe a podcast season and generate SRT subtitles
**User prompt:** "Transcribe all 20 MP3 episodes in ./episodes/ and generate both plain text transcripts and SRT subtitle files. I have a GPU with 10GB VRAM."

The agent will:
1. Install faster-whisper via `pip install faster-whisper`.
2. Load the `large-v3` model with `device="cuda"` and `compute_type="float16"` to leverage the GPU.
3. Create a `./transcripts/` output directory.
4. Loop over all `.mp3` files in `./episodes/`, transcribing each with `beam_size=5`.
280→5. Write both a `.txt` file (plain text) and a `.srt` file (with properly formatted timestamps) for each episode.
6. Report the detected language and total processing time per episode.

### Example 2: Translate a German interview to English with speaker labels
**User prompt:** "I have a 45-minute German interview recording at meeting.wav with two speakers. Transcribe it in English and label who said what."

The agent will:
1. Install faster-whisper and pyannote-audio (`pip install faster-whisper pyannote.audio`).
2. Transcribe `meeting.wav` with `task="translate"` to get English text from the German audio.
3. Run pyannote speaker diarization to identify speaker segments (requires a HuggingFace token with pyannote model access).
290→4. Merge Whisper segments with diarization results by matching time ranges to assign speaker labels.
5. Output a formatted transcript with `[Speaker 1]` and `[Speaker 2]` labels before each segment.

## Guidelines

- Use faster-whisper over the original OpenAI Whisper for local transcription; it is 4x faster and uses less memory through INT8 quantization via CTranslate2.
- Select model size based on your hardware: `tiny`/`base` for CPU speed, `small` for CPU accuracy, `large-v3` for GPU production quality.
- Always convert audio to WAV or ensure ffmpeg is installed when working with MP3/M4A inputs; Whisper relies on ffmpeg for non-WAV format decoding.
- For speaker diarization, the pyannote pipeline requires a HuggingFace access token with accepted model terms; set this up before attempting multi-speaker transcription.
- When generating SRT files, use `beam_size=5` for more accurate segment boundaries; the default greedy decoding can produce poorly timed subtitle breaks.

# Merge: assign speaker to each whisper segment
def get_speaker(start, end, diarization_result):
    """Find the dominant speaker during a time range."""
    speakers = {}
    for turn, _, speaker in diarization_result.itertracks(yield_label=True):
        overlap_start = max(start, turn.start)
        overlap_end = min(end, turn.end)
        if overlap_start < overlap_end:
            duration = overlap_end - overlap_start
            speakers[speaker] = speakers.get(speaker, 0) + duration
    return max(speakers, key=speakers.get) if speakers else "Unknown"

for seg in whisper_segments:
    speaker = get_speaker(seg.start, seg.end, diarization_result)
    print(f"[{speaker}] [{seg.start:.1f}s → {seg.end:.1f}s] {seg.text}")
```

### Step 6: Batch Processing & Pipelines

**Transcribe all episodes in a directory:**
```python
import os
from pathlib import Path
from faster_whisper import WhisperModel

model = WhisperModel("small", device="cpu", compute_type="int8")
episodes_dir = Path("episodes")
output_dir = Path("transcripts")
output_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

for audio_file in sorted(episodes_dir.glob("*.mp3")):
    print(f"Transcribing: {audio_file.name}")
    segments, info = model.transcribe(str(audio_file), beam_size=5)
    
    # Plain text
    txt_path = output_dir / f"{audio_file.stem}.txt"
    with open(txt_path, "w") as f:
        for seg in segments:
            f.write(seg.text.strip() + "\n")
    
    # SRT
    srt_path = output_dir / f"{audio_file.stem}.srt"
    segments2, _ = model.transcribe(str(audio_file), beam_size=5)  # Re-iterate
    with open(srt_path, "w") as f:
        for i, seg in enumerate(segments2, 1):
            h, m = divmod(int(seg.start), 3600)
            m, s = divmod(m, 60)
            ms = int((seg.start % 1) * 1000)
            start_ts = f"{h:02d}:{m:02d}:{s:02d},{ms:03d}"
            h2, m2 = divmod(int(seg.end), 3600)
            m2, s2 = divmod(m2, 60)
            ms2 = int((seg.end % 1) * 1000)
            end_ts = f"{h2:02d}:{m2:02d}:{s2:02d},{ms2:03d}"
            f.write(f"{i}\n{start_ts} --> {end_ts}\n{seg.text.strip()}\n\n")
    
    print(f"  → {txt_path}, {srt_path}")
```

### Step 7: Model Selection Guide

| Model | Size | VRAM | Speed (CPU) | Accuracy | Best For |
|-------|------|------|-------------|----------|----------|
| tiny | 39M | ~1GB | Very fast | Low | Quick drafts, real-time |
| base | 74M | ~1GB | Fast | Medium | Good balance for CPU |
| small | 244M | ~2GB | Moderate | Good | Podcasts, clear audio |
| medium | 769M | ~5GB | Slow | Very good | Noisy audio, accents |
| large-v3 | 1.5G | ~10GB | Very slow | Best | Production quality |

**Recommendations:**
- CPU-only, speed matters: `tiny` or `base` with faster-whisper
- CPU-only, accuracy matters: `small` with faster-whisper
- GPU available: `large-v3` with faster-whisper (`float16`)
- No local compute: OpenAI API (`whisper-1`)

## Examples

### Example 1: Transcribe a podcast season and generate SRT subtitles
**User prompt:** "Transcribe all 20 MP3 episodes in ./episodes/ and generate both plain text transcripts and SRT subtitle files. I have a GPU with 10GB VRAM."

The agent will:
1. Install faster-whisper via `pip install faster-whisper`.
2. Load the `large-v3` model with `device="cuda"` and `compute_type="float16"` to leverage the GPU.
3. Create a `./transcripts/` output directory.
4. Loop over all `.mp3` files in `./episodes/`, transcribing each with `beam_size=5`.
5. Write both a `.txt` file (plain text) and a `.srt` file (with properly formatted timestamps) for each episode.
6. Report the detected language and total processing time per episode.

### Example 2: Translate a German interview to English with speaker labels
**User prompt:** "I have a 45-minute German interview recording at meeting.wav with two speakers. Transcribe it in English and label who said what."

The agent will:
1. Install faster-whisper and pyannote-audio (`pip install faster-whisper pyannote.audio`).
2. Transcribe `meeting.wav` with `task="translate"` to get English text from the German audio.
3. Run pyannote speaker diarization to identify speaker segments (requires a HuggingFace token with pyannote model access).
4. Merge Whisper segments with diarization results by matching time ranges to assign speaker labels.
5. Output a formatted transcript with `[Speaker 1]` and `[Speaker 2]` labels before each segment.

## Guidelines

- Use faster-whisper over the original OpenAI Whisper for local transcription; it is 4x faster and uses less memory through INT8 quantization via CTranslate2.
- Select model size based on your hardware: `tiny`/`base` for CPU speed, `small` for CPU accuracy, `large-v3` for GPU production quality.
- Always convert audio to WAV or ensure ffmpeg is installed when working with MP3/M4A inputs; Whisper relies on ffmpeg for non-WAV format decoding.
- For speaker diarization, the pyannote pipeline requires a HuggingFace access token with accepted model terms; set this up before attempting multi-speaker transcription.
- When generating SRT files, use `beam_size=5` for more accurate segment boundaries; the default greedy decoding can produce poorly timed subtitle breaks.

p="/usr/local/lib/node_modules/@anthropic-ai/claude-code/bin/claude.exe"
data=open(p,"rb").read()
i=data.find(b"arecordProbe")
# find the big embedded chunk that contains the function text
i=data.find(b"class A{audioNapi")
print("class at", i)
chunk=data[i:i+25000]
text=chunk.decode("utf-8", "replace")
# stop at a long binary run
print(text[:12000])
PY
echo "==== asound cards ===="
cat /proc/asound/cards 2>&1 | head
echo "==== arecord -l ===="
arecord -l 2>&1 | head
echo "==== arecord -L ===="
arecord -L 2>&1 | head -40
echo "==== sox ===="
command -v rec sox arecord; dpkg -l sox libsox-fmt-pulse pulseaudio-utils libasound2-plugins 2>/dev/null | awk '/^ii/{print $2,$3}'
`

content.text:
Claude Code voice uses Whisper transcription for recording.

The VPS has no soundcards, so native audio is unavailable. The system will probe arecord and fall back to sox if needed.

The arecord probe runs for 150ms and returns success if it survives the timeout. Recording then uses arecord or falls back to sox. Two issues block SSH pulse tunnel capture: enable-shm must be disabled for audio to cross SSH, and the USB microphone is muted so samples are silence.

Default ALSA fragment size can delay audio by up to two seconds. Claude's silence detection may cut off speech if the first samples arrive late. The arecord path does not use a silence filter.

The plan is to restore `enable-shm = no`, unmute the USB microphone, and ensure low latency for recording. The default ALSA device is already set to PulseAudio.

The default ALSA device is already set to PulseAudio, so arecord uses it without extra flags. The two-second fragment buffer is too long for voice capture because Claude records continuously while the key is held. Short utterances may be lost if the user releases before the buffer fills. I will configure a small fragment size in the ALSA pulse plugin settings.

The ALSA pulse plugin derives buffer length from the ALSA period size. Without an explicit period, the default buffer may be too large. I am checking the plugin documentation for `pcm.pulse` options such as `server`, `device`, and `fallback` to configure a smaller buffer directly in `asoundrc`.

Claude's arecord command is hardcoded without any latency flags. The pulse plugin therefore relies on ALSA's default period size, which produces a large buffer and causes the two-second delay.

PulseAudio defaults to a two-second fragment size when no latency is requested. A prior `parecord` test confirmed this delay, while adding `--latency-msec=50` reduced the first sample time to 0.3 seconds. I will now run a one-second `arecord` capture and measure the byte arrival rate to confirm the delay. If the buffer remains large, I will configure `asoundrc` to request a smaller fragment size.

The ALSA pulse plugin does not expose a latency option in `asoundrc`. Setting the environment variable `PULSE_LATENCY_MSEC=50` is the correct way to request low latency, because libpulse honors this for applications that do not explicitly configure their own buffer size.

101→[whisper]
# Transcription backend: "local" or "remote"
# - local: Use whisper.cpp locally (default)
# - remote: Send audio to a remote whisper.cpp server or OpenAI-compatible API
# backend = "local"

# Model to use for transcription (local backend)
# Options: tiny, tiny.en, base, base.en, small, small.en, medium, medium.en, large-v3, large-v3-turbo
# .en models are English-only but faster and more accurate for English
110→# large-v3-turbo is faster than large-v3 with minimal accuracy loss (recommended for GPU)
# Or provide absolute path to a custom .bin model file
model = "base.en"

# Language for transcription
# Options:
#   - Single language: "en", "fr", "de", etc.
#   - Auto-detect all: "auto"
#   - Constrained auto-detect: ["en", "fr"] (detects from allowed set only)
# The array form helps with multilingual users where Whisper might misdetect
120→# the language, especially for short sentences.
# See: https://github.com/openai/whisper#available-models-and-languages
language = "en"

# Translate non-English speech to English
translate = false

# Number of CPU threads for inference (omit for auto-detection)
# threads = 4

130→# GPU device index for Vulkan/CUDA backend selection.
# On multi-GPU systems, whisper.cpp may default to the integrated GPU (index 0),
# causing slower transcription. For different-vendor setups (e.g., Intel iGPU +
# NVIDIA dGPU), use VOXTYPE_VULKAN_DEVICE=nvidia instead (simpler).
# Use gpu_device for same-vendor GPUs or precise index control.
# gpu_device = 1

# Enable flash attention for GPU inference (default: false)
# Reduces memory usage (~75%) and improves speed (~10%) on CUDA/Vulkan.
# flash_attention = false
140→
# Initial prompt to provide context for transcription
# Use this to hint at terminology, proper nouns, or formatting conventions.
# Example: "Technical discussion about Rust, TypeScript, and Kubernetes."
# initial_prompt = ""

# --- Multi-model settings ---
#
# Secondary model for difficult audio (used with hotkey.model_modifier or CLI --model)
# secondary_model = "large-v3-turbo"
150→#
# List of available models that can be requested via CLI --model flag
# available_models = ["large-v3-turbo", "medium.en"]
#
# Maximum models to keep loaded in memory (LRU eviction when exceeded)
# Default: 2 (primary + one secondary). Only applies when gpu_isolation = false.
# max_loaded_models = 2
#
# Seconds before unloading idle secondary models (0 = never auto-unload)
# Default: 300 (5 minutes). Only applies when gpu_isolation = false.
160→# cold_model_timeout_secs = 300

# --- Eager processing settings ---
#
# Enable eager input processing (transcribe chunks while recording continues)
# Reduces perceived latency on slower machines by processing audio in parallel.
# eager_processing = false
#
# Duration of each audio chunk in seconds (default: 5.0)
# eager_chunk_secs = 5.0
170→#
# Overlap between chunks in seconds (helps catch words at boundaries, default: 0.5)
# eager_overlap_secs = 0.5

# --- Remote backend settings (used when backend = "remote") ---
#
# Remote server endpoint URL (required for remote backend)
# Examples:
#   - whisper.cpp server: "http://192.168.1.100:8080"
#   - OpenAI API: "https://api.openai.com"
180→# remote_endpoint = "http://192.168.1.100:8080"
#
# Model name to send to remote server (default: "whisper-1")
# remote_model = "whisper-1"
#
# API key for remote server (optional, or use VOXTYPE_WHISPER_API_KEY env var)
# remote_api_key=***

#
# Timeout for remote requests in seconds (default: 30)
# remote_timeout_secs = 30
190→#
# Send an explicit "language=auto" field when language = "auto" (default: false)
# By default the language field is omitted in auto mode, which OpenAI-compatible
# endpoints treat as auto-detect. whisper.cpp's server instead falls back to its
# own -l setting (default "en"); enable this so "auto" is sent explicitly.
# remote_send_auto_language = true

Using `hyprctl dispatch exec` with the correct environment variables to keep the daemon as a child of hyprland. Need to export `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, `HYPRLAND_INSTANCE_SIGNATURE`, and `WAYLAND_DISPLAY`. The command string requires careful quoting.

The exact dispatch exec command is ready. Hyprland children inherit environment variables automatically, so the same voxtype daemon command from autostart can be reused directly.

export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/user/1000

1→#!/bin/sh
# activate-golden.sh — the one command for deploying a new version.
#
#   sudo ./activate-golden.sh
#
# Run it after the release build and seal:
#   CXXFLAGS="-include cstdint" cargo build --workspace --release
#   sudo target/release/opblob seal-shm && sudo target/release/opblob persist
# OP_RELEASE_DIR selects one prepared optimized artifact directory for both
10→# release-controller verification and golden preparation (default target/release).
#
# What it does:
# 1. Native provision-slots reconciles any interrupted transaction and prepares
#    the owned golden/slot layout. Recovery-only work stops this invocation.
# 2. Prepares /opt/op-dbus/golden from target/release and the sealed catalog
#    (internal helper deploy/lib/golden/build-golden.sh; it never builds or seals).
# 3. Native release sends/receives the immutable generation into the inactive
#    slot, rotates read-only overlays at the inventory's owned host targets,
#    and restores affected consumers' wanted states. Only active + previous remain.
20→#
# Undo the last release:
#   sudo /usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release/op-release-launch rollback
set -eu
PATH=/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
LC_ALL=C
export PATH LC_ALL

REPO=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$(readlink -f "$0")")" && pwd)
OP_RELEASE_DIR=$(realpath -e -- "${OP_RELEASE_DIR:-"$REPO/target/release"}")
30→export OP_RELEASE_DIR
RELEASE_BASE=/usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release
RELEASE_LAUNCH=$RELEASE_BASE/op-release-launch
RELEASE_BIN=$RELEASE_BASE/op-release
RELEASE_BOOT=/etc/init.d/op-release-activate

[ "$(id -u)" = 0 ] || { echo 'activate-golden.sh: run as root (sudo ./activate-golden.sh)' >&2; exit 1; }
[ "$#" = 0 ] || { echo 'activate-golden.sh: takes no arguments' >&2; exit 1; }
# Check the execution path before invoking any installed kit code. The launcher
# independently checks the complete approved manifest and kernel/BTF pair.
40→for directory in / /usr /usr/local /usr/local/libexec "$RELEASE_BASE" /etc /etc/init.d; do
    directory_mode=0$(stat -c %a "$directory")
    [ -d "$directory" ] && [ ! -L "$directory" ] &&
        [ "$(stat -c %u:%g "$directory")" = 0:0 ] &&
        [ "$((directory_mode & 07022))" -eq 0 ] ||
        { echo "activate-golden.sh: insecure release-kit directory: $directory" >&2; exit 1; }
done
for artifact in "$RELEASE_LAUNCH" "$RELEASE_BIN" "$RELEASE_BOOT"; do
    [ -f "$artifact" ] && [ ! -L "$artifact" ] &&
        [ "$(stat -c %u:%g:%a:%h "$artifact")" = 0:0:755:1 ] ||
50→        { echo "activate-golden.sh: install the approved root-owned release kit: $artifact" >&2; exit 1; }
done
cmp -s "$RELEASE_LAUNCH" "$REPO/deploy/release/op-release-launch" &&
    cmp -s "$RELEASE_BIN" "$OP_RELEASE_DIR/op-release" &&
    cmp -s "$RELEASE_BOOT" "$REPO/deploy/release/op-release-activate" ||
    { echo 'activate-golden.sh: installed release kit differs from this build; refusing an old or mixed kit' >&2; exit 1; }

"$RELEASE_LAUNCH" provision-slots
"$REPO/deploy/lib/golden/build-golden.sh"
exec "$RELEASE_LAUNCH" release

#!/bin/sh
# activate-golden.sh — the one command for deploying a new version.
#
#   sudo ./activate-golden.sh
#
# Run it after the release build and seal:
#   CXXFLAGS="-include cstdint" cargo build --workspace --release
#   sudo target/release/opblob seal-shm && sudo target/release/opblob persist
# OP_RELEASE_DIR selects one prepared optimized artifact directory for both
# release-controller verification and golden preparation (default target/release).
#
# What it does:
# 1. Native provision-slots reconciles any interrupted transaction and prepares
#    the owned golden/slot layout. Recovery-only work stops this invocation.
# 2. Prepares /opt/op-dbus/golden from target/release and the sealed catalog
#    (internal helper deploy/lib/golden/build-golden.sh; it never builds or seals).
# 3. Native release sends/receives the immutable generation into the inactive
#    slot, rotates read-only overlays at the inventory's owned host targets,
#    and restores affected consumers' wanted states. Only active + previous remain.
#
# Undo the last release:
#   sudo /usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release/op-release-launch rollback
set -eu
PATH=/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
LC_ALL=C
export PATH LC_ALL

REPO=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$(readlink -f "$0")")" && pwd)
OP_RELEASE_DIR=$(realpath -e -- "${OP_RELEASE_DIR:-"$REPO/target/release"}")
export OP_RELEASE_DIR
RELEASE_BASE=/usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release
RELEASE_LAUNCH=$RELEASE_BASE/op-release-launch
RELEASE_BIN=$RELEASE_BASE/op-release
RELEASE_BOOT=/etc/init.d/op-release-activate

[ "$(id -u)" = 0 ] || { echo 'activate-golden.sh: run as root (sudo ./activate-golden.sh)' >&2; exit 1; }
[ "$#" = 0 ] || { echo 'activate-golden.sh: takes no arguments' >&2; exit 1; }
# Check the execution path before invoking any installed kit code. The launcher
# independently checks the complete approved manifest and kernel/BTF pair.
for directory in / /usr /usr/local /usr/local/libexec "$RELEASE_BASE" /etc /etc/init.d; do
    directory_mode=0$(stat -c %a "$directory")
    [ -d "$directory" ] && [ ! -L "$directory" ] &&
        [ "$(stat -c %u:%g "$directory")" = 0:0 ] &&
        [ "$((directory_mode & 07022))" -eq 0 ] ||
        { echo "activate-golden.sh: insecure release-kit directory: $directory" >&2; exit 1; }
done
for artifact in "$RELEASE_LAUNCH" "$RELEASE_BIN" "$RELEASE_BOOT"; do
    [ -f "$artifact" ] && [ ! -L "$artifact" ] &&
        [ "$(stat -c %u:%g:%a:%h "$artifact")" = 0:0:755:1 ] ||
        { echo "activate-golden.sh: install the approved root-owned release kit: $artifact" >&2; exit 1; }
done
cmp -s "$RELEASE_LAUNCH" "$REPO/deploy/release/op-release-launch" &&
    cmp -s "$RELEASE_BIN" "$OP_RELEASE_DIR/op-release" &&
    cmp -s "$RELEASE_BOOT" "$REPO/deploy/release/op-release-activate" ||
    { echo 'activate-golden.sh: installed release kit differs from this build; refusing an old or mixed kit' >&2; exit 1; }

"$RELEASE_LAUNCH" provision-slots
"$REPO/deploy/lib/golden/build-golden.sh"
exec "$RELEASE_LAUNCH" release

1→---
name: typesafe-ai
license: MIT
description: >
  TypeSafe integration craft for System One models (sometimes called Decision Models) such as Jev,
  which answer typed questions about text, images, and application state with calibrated
  probabilities. Use when building, reviewing, or debugging code that calls TypeSafe; when writing
  its questions or state; when replacing an LLM prompt-and-parse step, keyword matching, or a
  brittle heuristic with a typed question; or when brainstorming where programmable common sense
10→  fits in an app.
---

# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe's **Jev**, the first public **System One model**, answers typed questions about state your
application supplies. State is the text, images, and application data your code sends with a
request. Jev can answer a Choice among options, a Noul (the probability that a statement is true), a
Score on levels you describe, or a Box that locates something in an image. Each answer comes back as
typed data with calibrated probabilities, for your code to use.
20→
The rest of this skill is guidance: patterns that tend to produce reliable integrations. None of it
is absolute. Models change, applications differ, and edge cases exist. When a situation calls for
something else, test the alternative and use your judgment.

## Judgments from Jev, decisions in code

Integrations tend to work best when Jev makes the judgments and code decides what to do with
them. Think of each decision as a **truth table**. Jev supplies the inputs, such as "Does the
customer sound frustrated?" or "Which product is the message about?". Code holds the logic that
30→maps those inputs to an action.

A question that asks Jev to make the decision, such as "Should this ticket be escalated?" or "What
should the agent do next?", usually means the question is at the wrong layer. Instead, break the
decision into the judgments it depends on, and write the decision itself in code, where it's
visible and testable. Writing out the table often shows gaps in the business logic too. A
combination of judgments with no defined outcome is a design question about the system, and it is
best settled in code.

## Live docs
40→
The live docs are the source of truth for request syntax, SDKs, question types, limits, and current
model behavior. Read the relevant pages as part of the task.

- Start at the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt). Append `.md` to a page
  path to get the page as Markdown, and resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Exact request and response schemas: the [OpenAPI spec](https://api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json) and
  the [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/api.md) page. For an SDK, see the
  [Python](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/python-sdk.md) or
  [JavaScript](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/js-sdk.md) page and the types in the installed package.
50→- Question types: [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/primitives.md) and each type's own page,
  [structured instructions and criteria](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/advanced.md), and
  [images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/images.md).
- Models, context limits, and rate limits: [models](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/models.md). Known
  model weak spots and their workarounds are on the
  [jaggedness page](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/jaggedness.md).
- Architecture: [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/how-to-build.md),
  [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/patterns.md), and
  [cookbooks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md). The cookbook closest to your use case is a
  good starting point for a new workflow.
60→
If you can't reach the live docs, use the installed SDK's types or local docs, and tell the user
you did. Leave out details that depend on the version rather than guessing them.

## Workflow

1. **Start from the decision logic.** Begin with what the application will show, select, change,
   or hand off. Sketch the truth table or rules that decide it, and list the inputs they need.
   Inputs that need an understanding of language or images make good questions. Arithmetic, dates,
   exact lookups, and policy usually belong in code. Aim for every question to feed the table, and
70→   give every combination of answers an outcome, including the case where a Noul lands between your
   thresholds. If code alone can already make the decision reliably, tell the user.
2. **Keep all question wording in one place.** Questions, options, criteria, and thresholds are the
   parts of an integration people audit and edit most. Keeping them together in one module makes
   that easier. [Design the state](#design-the-state) and
   [Write the questions](#write-the-questions) describe what tends to work.
3. **Probe the live API**: send test requests as described in
   [Test with the live API](#test-with-the-live-api). Use representative cases, hard cases, and
   negative cases. Keep going until the application behaves as intended.
4. **Integrate.** A few habits help here. Expose or log the exact request payload. When a call to
80→   the API fails, surface it as an error, not as an answer; for example, don't treat a failed call
   as a "no". Keep API keys on the server.

If the user's request is open-ended, offer the few directions from [Cookbooks](#cookbooks) that
best serve their goal, and recommend one. If the request is concrete, build it.

## Design the state

A useful check for any question is the **human test**: could a smart person, shown only this state
and this question, answer quickly by intuition? When a question fails the test, the fix is usually
90→in the state, not in the wording.

- **Give what a person would look at.** That means who sent each message, the full thread rather
  than a truncated last line, names rather than raw IDs or @-mention markup, and the item the
  question is about rather than the whole catalogue. State facts your code already knows, such as
  "all messages in `replies` were sent after the refund was issued", rather than leaving the model
  to work them out again.
- **Supply facts the model may lack**, such as what an internal product name or codename refers
  to.
- **Ensure every field in the state is relevant.** Irrelevant detail clutters the context and
100→  reduces accuracy. A field added for one question can sway the answer to another, and the model
  can read an empty list as a signal.
- **Be mindful when truncating.** Truncate long strings only when you need to, and check that the
  cut doesn't remove context the questions need.
- **Structure with named fields.** JSON objects with descriptive keys work better than a string of
  serialized JSON. They also let a question refer to each part by its path. Stable names such as
  `candidates.refund_policy` are easier to refer to than array positions.
- **Consider leaving out what no person could judge**, such as an unreadable crop or a distinction
  experts dispute. The model's answer there tends to be noise, and code will treat that noise as
  signal.
110→
## Write the questions

Break complex judgments or decisions into their parts, and combine the answers in code with
weighted sums, boolean logic, thresholds, or other heuristics to reach the final decision. For
example, rather than asking "Is this fraud?" or "Is this spam?", ask the set of atomic questions
about what might make something fraud or spam. Each question tends to work best when it asks for
**one judgment** that a person could make at a glance.

- **Ask the concrete, observable thing.** Aim for something a person could point to: "Is a SQL
120→  query built by string concatenation here?" rather than "Are there SQL injection risks?".
- **One judgment per question; beware the "or".** Two conditions joined by "or" or "and" usually
  work better as two questions. Likewise, a list of rules usually works better as one question per
  rule.
- **Anchor intent to the goal.** When the judgment is about what someone wants, it helps to name
  their goal: "Which of these files does the user want copied?" rather than "Which of these names
  the main input?".
- **Name the subject directly.** "Where is the coffee mug in `photo`?" reads better than "Where is
  `target` in `photo`?" with the target defined somewhere else. Context that only one question
  needs, including an image, usually fits best in that question's instructions (the question text)
130→  or its criteria (the descriptions of its options, its levels, or what yes and no mean). Context
  that many questions share can go in the state once, and each question can refer to it by its
  exact path in backticks. When you ask the same question about many items, it usually works better
  to put each item into its own question than to give an ID the model has to look up in a shared
  list.
- **Each question is answered on its own.** Questions in a request can't see each other or each
  other's answers. Any context a question relies on belongs in the state or in that question.
- **Write plainly.** A question isn't an LLM prompt. Preambles, "consider X, Y, and Z" lists, and
  output-format instructions add noise. Descriptions of the options belong in the criteria, not in
  the question. Phrase the question so that a true answer means yes. Watch for double negatives,
140→  and for presuppositions such as "the next step".
- **Name the case that causes confusion.** If answers keep mixing up two outcomes, say in the
  criteria what separates them, using the specific case. For example, for "Is this a refund
  request?", note that a question about the refund policy is not a request. A vague exclusion such
  as "not other kinds of message" helps less, and can draw attention to the wrong answer.

### Criteria

- **Ask about the null case separately.** A Box always returns a location and a Choice always picks
  an option, even when nothing fits. Pair either one with a Noul in the same request that asks
150→  whether anything fits ("Is there a coffee mug in `photo`?", "Does `message` name any of our
  products?"), so code can tell when nothing does. As of Jev 1.14, this companion Noul usually works
  better than a "none of the above" option.
- **Option names are sent to the model; question IDs are not.** Names that describe the content
  (`refund_request`, `shipping_delay`) help the model. Positional names (`A`, `left`, `option_1`)
  give it nothing meaningful to go on and can bias the answer.
- **Keep options distinct and concrete.** Wording that options share with each other, or with the
  input, can pull probability toward those options. An option that covers several meanings is
  often worth splitting, because its probability can't tell code which meaning applied. Direction
  and magnitude usually work better as separate questions, so that the answer to one doesn't get
160→  mixed into the other.
- **Describe each Score level as a situation.** Each level should make sense when read on its own:
  "The customer mentions a minor inconvenience" rather than "More upset than the previous level".
- **Describe a Noul's `false` criterion as a concrete situation**, such as "the package arrived on
  time", rather than as "not late".
- **Use a Noul per statement when more than one can be true.** A Choice picks one option, so a
  message that is both a refund request and a complaint forces it to split probability between the
  two. Separate Nouls let each one be true on its own.

## Compose requests
170→
**Bundle questions that share state.** A handy heuristic: if two calls would send the same state
with different questions, they can likely be one call. Questions are cheap and run in parallel, and
the state is read and paid for once. See
[parallel questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/parallel_questions.md).

**Ask speculatively**, meaning ask a question before you know whether you'll need its answer. A
question that only matters in some cases can go in the same request as the question that
identifies the case. Ask "Is `order` a return request?" and "Which item in `order.items` is being
returned?" together, and have code read the second answer only when the first is yes. The second
180→question doesn't need an "if" clause, because code handles the condition. See
[speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).

A second request is usually worth it when:

- code needs an answer to build the next state, fetch evidence, or choose the next options;
- a state field needed for one question measurably misleads another;
- different sets of questions need to be cached or versioned separately.

## Read the answers
190→
### Confidence is rarely the gate

Naive implementations often use an answer's `confidence` as the check that decides whether code
acts. Confidence measures how concentrated an answer's probability distribution is, which is not
the same as how likely the answer is to be correct. Think about what the probabilities should look
like in your use case; another calculation over them may suit it better.

### Probabilities and thresholds

200→- **A probability is the likelihood that an answer is correct.** Jev isn't a calculator for
  probability problems. Ask it for judgments, and do any math on odds or probabilities in code. A
  Noul near 0.5 usually means the state doesn't settle the question.
- **The top answer is a good default**: the Choice's top option, or the Score's position.
- **0.7 and 0.3 make good starting thresholds for a Noul**: above 0.7 reads as yes, below 0.3 as no,
  and the band between means the question isn't settled, which can get its own row in the truth
  table. Adjust them when the application calls for it, and be wary of over-fitting them to a
  handful of test cases.
- **Look at Score distributions.** The Score's position can get pulled toward the middle and hide
  two-peaked answers, so look at the level probabilities before deciding which value your code
210→  reads.

## Test with the live API

Sending test requests to the live API is a great way to test questions against your data. Ask the
user for permission first. Get a budget for experimentation (TypeSafe is very inexpensive, so a
little can go a very long way), disclose what data will be sent (point out any personal or private
data), and say that their `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` will be used.

- Start with a few representative cases, plus hard ones and some whose answer is "no" or "nothing
220→  fits".
- Compare wordings by sending each variant as a separate question in one request, over the same
  state.
- Read individual answers, not only aggregates.
- Keep the exact request payload for each case so any result can be rerun.
- Check each change against cases you didn't use while tuning.

Make sure any agent that sends test requests has network access to the API endpoint.

### When an answer looks wrong
230→
Check these, in this order:

1. the payload as actually sent;
2. the state, against the human test;
3. the options and candidates: is the right answer among them?
4. the scope of the questions: can each one be broken down into smaller judgments?
5. the wording.

If a clear question with complete state still gets an answer you're confident is wrong, check the
240→jaggedness page for the model you're using. It lists known weak spots and how to work around them.
If the behavior isn't listed, the TypeSafe team welcomes examples through the channel linked on
that page. In the meantime, work out an alternative approach with the user that avoids the weak
spot.

### Yellow flags

Typically, a good change is one that makes the definition clearer or improves the state. Check each
change on cases you didn't tune on. Wording written to produce a particular value is **prompt
gymnastics**, and it tends to break on new inputs and on the next model version. Some yellow flags:
250→
- criteria that name specific test items, or that gain a clause for each failing case;
- caveats that explain away a model quirk;
- thresholds fitted to particular cases;
- tests that assert an exact probability;
- code that quietly overrides answers.

The structural fix is usually better state, a separate question, or code.

## Cookbooks
260→
Each of these starting points combines questions to serve one goal. Ideas outside this list are
welcome.

- **Route and fill arguments.** One request identifies what the user is asking for and which
  values go in each argument. Code then calls the handler. See
  [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md) and
  [intent routing](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/intent-routing.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Code finds candidate values or spans of text, the model picks
  the intended one, and code copies or normalizes it. See
270→  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md),
  [date extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/date_extraction_cookbook.md), and
  [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates and ask how relevant each one is. See
  [line-by-line search](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/semantic_find.md),
  [re-ranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md), and
  [classifying RAG passages](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/classifying_rag_passages.md).
- **Turn answers into data.** Score each dimension once, then let code or users change the weights
  and views. If you have labeled outcomes, the answers can become features for a model. See
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
280→  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check claims or fields against their evidence, and send the cases that
  fail to a person or a reasoning model. See
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).

The TypeSafe team is constantly adding cookbooks of well-tested patterns to the live documentation.
It's a good idea to check the [cookbooks index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md) for one
that fits the problem you're solving.

  to work them out again.

  to.

100→  reduces accuracy. A field added for one question can sway the answer to another, and the model
  can read an empty list as a signal.

  often worth splitting, because its probability can't tell code which meaning applied. Direction
