Never modify a seed while retained leaves depend on it. Older add-on-start/remove-on-stop guidance in source, handoffs and signals is superseded; do not restore it. Host release snapshot/send/receive below is a separate deployment mechanism.
- **D-Bus is the only control plane.** Every plugin is a D-Bus object at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>` under `org.opdbus.v1`. No `Command::new(...)` subprocesses, no direct file reads for live state, no polling loops in plugin/service code. New backend capabilities register as plugins in `crates/op-plugins/src/default_registry.rs` — never as new gRPC proto service packages.
- **The plugin IS the schema — one source of truth, nonnegotiable.** That single schema is sealed into the blob, which IS the plugin. D-Bus method signatures, 3tchedFS operation files, gRPC shapes, and UI field renderers derive from it. Validate inputs against it. Each plugin defines its schema under `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/`, using `plugin_scaffold_helpers.rs`. **There must be no parallel plugin schema source in a repository-level or plugin `schemas/` directory.** The former plugin capture directories, separate section files, and JSON-file loader have been removed. `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/schema_loader.rs` still exists by name, but it reads only a manifest-pinned `PluginSchema` from the sealed blob catalog; it is not a file-schema fallback. **Owner correction (2026-10-18): capture threetched's full `config schema` from the verified binary on every seal.** The shared capture fixes the runtime config directory, checks the binary and manifest, and supplies native_config, MCP, model_routes, plugins and skill_bundles. `tched_router_contract.rs` contains only access/section helpers; the embedded UPSTREAM IMPORT is retired. Build-time generated bridge contracts explicitly prepare the same capture; runtime consumes the sealed catalog and never starts capture as a fallback. Do not restore an embedded schema or add independent captures using the sealer's ambient environment. The per-section generator and generated surface were retired on 2026-10-04. Older docs claiming a single `plugin_schema_defs.rs` are also stale — that file does not exist.
- **The sealed blob IS the plugin.** Present state lives in the sealed blob catalog at `/dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs/<plugin_id>.<schema_hash16>.blob`. A plugin exists ⟺ its blob is in the catalog. The sole writer is the blob sealer in `op-blob`. Consumers read SHM directly (zero-copy) — they never re-hash and never consult the Rust registry for existence. The old `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas` folder and `live-schema.json` are gone.
- **MutationEngine owns state; streaming comes from SHM (owner reaffirmed 2026-09-13).** MutationEngine folds authoritative backend results into the complete state tree, including child objects, and commits that state to canonical SHM before change notifications. Child updates/deletions must preserve unrelated children and parent fields. Existing subscriptions derive their values from committed SHM; an in-memory event payload, method argument, or generator buffer is not a second state authority. Preserve verified principal/session scope for private state. Do not add a separate per-method streaming control plane or claim a buffered unary response provides state streaming.
- **MCP retired — initial setup error (owner correction 2026-10-28).** There is no MCP interface. MCP was part of the initial setup in error and has been replaced by 3tchedFS: an identity reads and calls sealed methods only through its own mounted namespace (`operations/<plugin>/<method>/call`), admitted and receipted by the bridge. Do not build on, document as current, or re-enable the bridge's `/mcp` endpoint, the leftover `3tched-fs mcp` subcommand, router MCP bundles, or in-process cognitive/compact MCP. The former text ("MCP gateway (settled): one public MCP door on `:8090`…, compact mode 4 meta-tools in op-web…") is superseded. Never create new shims or point external clients at `op-assistant-grpc`.
- **External binaries back plugins; the plugin remains the single schema source.** 3tched-router / tched-router (`tched_router` in code) is the framework/schema/plugin integration backed by the autonomous `/usr/bin/threetched` executable. The reproducible threetched input is pinned in `vendor/tched-router/source.pin`; `vendor/tched-router/build-threetched.sh` applies the checked-in patches and emits `target/threetched-artifacts/tched-router/{threetched,manifest.json}` without installing it. `build-golden.sh` validates the pin, patch and binary provenance, then stages the binary, `/usr/share/op-dbus/threetched-manifests/tched-router.json`, `/etc/op-dbus/threetched-runtime.toml`, and the tracked default skill bundle into the golden filesystem. The `tched-router` runit service verifies that manifest, exact commit, binary digest, and version before exec, then seeds its private runtime config and skills from those staged bootstrap files. A fresh checkout includes the digest-pinned upstream source archive, patches and build recipe; the helper verifies and uses that archive by default. Cargo registry dependencies and system build tools still need provisioning. Owner correction (2026-10-11): the executable and runtime-facing branding are lowercase `threetched`; the FUSE discovery source is `threetched-surface.rs`. Preserve upstream repository URLs, licenses and historical provenance. The former instruction to keep the executable named zeroclaw is superseded. The plugin contract remains `tched_router_contract.rs`, and source attribution may identify `zeroclaw config schema`.
- **Owner-confirmed lifecycle and model roles (2026-09-13, reaffirmed 2026-09-14).** Waypipe is retired: its crate directory, Cargo membership, binary target and protocol are absent; `retired-binaries`/`retired-services` prevent stale build or service artifacts from entering golden. Do not restore it in source exports or release inputs. Assistant is the control-plane chatbot, not an `assistant` container. The historical Gemma routing role is model agnostic; the `op-gemma` crate is retired (2026-09-19: directory, Cargo membership and binary removed, listed in `retired-binaries`) — the `gemma_brain` plugin remains and its role does not constrain the model/provider. Cargo membership and legacy names do not establish active deployments.
- **Factory role correction (2026-09-14).** The former Factory account/platform plugin is retired from the registry and dispatch. The intended access is CLI/SSH; routing belongs to `tched_router`, and Factory billing requires an actual native binding. Provider names or relabelled direct upstream routes do not prove that binding. A future Missions integration needs its own verified native contract; do not restore the retired REST platform methods from historical fixtures or docs.
- **Standalone vendor adapters are retired (2026-09-14).** The `op-grpc-adapters` crate directory and its `op.adapters.v1` protocol are absent after Netmaker retirement. Its duplicate mail/MQ services bypassed canonical plugin admission. Do not restore this crate or its old Netmaker clients. The existing bridge `operation.mail.v1` service and retained EMQX plugin are separate surfaces; their presence does not prove every mail or MQTT method is implemented.
- **Identity minting and metadata (owner reaffirmed 2026-09-13).** The identity subsystem owns minting the identity and its SealedId/SID1 credential blob. This is distinct from an OPBLOB01 plugin blob and does not belong in the plugin catalog. Clients forward the authored credential through the transport's identity metadata; they do not mint or reconstruct it from genesis/trace/key headers. Verify minting, persistence, injection and receiver validation as separate links. Current source assigns session/SID1 creation to MutationEngine with the op-identity format; the existence of an HTTP/MCP helper does not prove every gRPC client injects SID1.
- **Identity injection (owner decision 2026-09-25).** The decoy mints the sealed identity blob; the 8090 interceptor anchors the session and writes the identity metadata (`anchor_verified_human_session` and `insert_identity_metadata` in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/interceptor.rs`). The oracle (OIA1) is the decoy's signed peer proof; the human credential (SID1) is the session identity for that key. The bridge's own client and MutationEngine are the wrong place for session or identity injection. Source and live state did not match this on 2026-09-25: the interceptor still mints genesis server-side when no session exists (`mint_and_store_genesis` in `anchor_verified_human_session`), and the decoy issuer mints only OIA1. Transport paths (decoy, WARP, door addresses) are in `docs/src/operations/network.md`.
- **Btrfs storage and transport (owner correction 2026-09-23).** Deployment remains the prepared snapshot transferred by `btrfs send/receive`. The earlier global five-subvolume limit and instruction to replace Snowball/cache subvolumes with ordinary directories are withdrawn. Preserve the original `operation-dbus-proto` cache/NUMA/timing architecture: Btrfs cache category subvolumes; authoritative timing plus vector/state subvolumes; aligned read-only snapshot sets and send/receive. See the original repo `branding/product-baseline.md` §12 and `crates/op-snowball/{DESIGN,REQUIREMENTS}.md` (R5). Retention is configurable per storage owner, not a global five-subvolume cap. Parent snapshots do not include nested subvolume contents: snapshot and transport every required member explicitly. Never flatten existing subvolumes or delete historical data to satisfy the withdrawn limit. Preserve security, writer-locking, identity and error-handling fixes while correcting storage regressions.
- **No SQLite — use CozoDB.** CozoDB (`op-cozo-store`) is the embedded database for this project. Do not add new `rusqlite` or other SQLite use. `op-cache/src/btrfs_cache.rs` already uses a Cozo index; current `workstack_cache.rs`, `workflow_cache.rs`, `workflow_tracker.rs`, and `pattern_tracker.rs` still use `rusqlite` and remain migration debt rather than an approved pattern.
- **RAG pipeline and Voyage-4 models.** Live source file indexing goes through `code_index` (mode='source') into Qdrant collections: `repos_lsp_*_voyage_4_large` and `repos_lsp_*_voyage_4_lite`. Voyage-4 models are interchangeable across their dimension (1024 for all variants); `_large` and `_lite` refer to model size/quality tier, not embedding space. All collections share a single fused retrieval space and can be queried together. Legacy `repos_lsp_*_voyage_code_4` collections and `repomix_rag` collection are retired — do not use them. The standalone `notebooklm-mcp` service is retired; the plugin-owned `notebooklm` contract and bridge provider remain. Owner reaffirmed NotebookLM conversation/tool-history sync on 2026-10-05; use its declared methods through identity-bound 3tchedFS. Do not confuse this corpus sync with the Voyage source-indexing pipeline.

## Handoff between agents

Claude, Codex, Grok and any other agent share one handoff: `HANDOFF.md`. Read it
at the start of every session, after this file. Claim your task in its *Active
work* table before changing anything, and never reset, stash or overwrite work
another agent has claimed there. Before the session ends, or before a context or
usage limit, update your row and add a dated *Handoff* entry. A handoff kept only
in one agent's private memory is invisible to the others, so it does not count.

## Signals and task board

- **Append observations to `SIGNALS.md`** rather than letting them evaporate in chat. Three signal types: `💡 SUGGESTION` · `⚠️ CONCERN` · `👁️ OBSERVATION`. Each row: date · model · signal · optional `→ OD-##` link. Models leave status `open`. Promote anything actionable to `WISHLIST.md` as an `OD-##` and link it back.
- **`WISHLIST.md` is the canonical task board** — do not create new TODO docs. Priority buckets: Critical/Urgent → Current → Next → Future → When I Have Staff. Dispatch syntax: "dispatch <ID> to <agent>" spawns an agent with the task context and updates status here.
- **Read recent `SIGNALS.md` rows before non-trivial work** in the area they touch — the file records load-bearing gotchas (stale vendored deps, live/deployed drift, the live-vs-intent identity topology) that source alone will not surface.

## Stale documentation

- **README.md is stale**: crate count (31) is wrong, `cd lovable` is a deleted directory, `sudo service6` references are retired. Prefer AGENTS.md and source over README claims.
- Many older deploy scripts and HANDOFF docs still reference s6 — treat them as archival; runit/`sv` is current.
- Anything mentioning `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat`, `live-schema.json`, or `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas` is describing a retired design.
- Anything mentioning `OIB1`, `oib1:`, `blob_ref`, `SessionIdentityBlob`, or `x-opdbus-identity-blob-bin` is pre-2026-09-01 and stale; the session-identity envelope is now `SID1` / `SealedId`.
- Anything referencing `crates/op-web/ui/`, `zeroclaw-gui`, pairing codes, or `operation-dashboard-ui-07` — the production UI is `/srv/git/3tched.com` (github.com/repr0bated/3tched.com), deployed from that repo through `scripts/publish-op-web.sh`. `LANDING` selects the mount name; `URL_PREFIX=/` selects the dashboard root.
- Older deployment-script and backup/restore hierarchy descriptions are not current deployment authority. Deployment is btrfs send/receive of the prepared snapshot — see architecture invariants above.

## Subagent and model selection

Cargo execution follows JEV routing above; the guidance below does not allocate
Cargo models.

**Owner preference (2026-09-13, model names withdrawn 2026-09-24,
reaffirmed 2026-09-30): assess task
difficulty and required reasoning before delegation, and use the cheapest
available model that can complete it at the same quality.** A lower price must
not thin the answer, skip evidence, or weaken a judgment. If the cheaper model
would lose accuracy, completeness, or care, use the more capable model. Pick
from the models the session can actually launch. Do not inherit an expensive
parent model by default, and do not pin a product or model id in this file.
Use a low-cost model for lookups, inventory extraction, documentation
assembly and routine non-Cargo checks when that model can match the
quality of a more capable one. Choose low effort for mechanical work and
medium effort for bounded reasoning. Escalate when the task's quality needs
it or a cheaper attempt falls short, and briefly state why.

Keep the primary agent available for user communication and coordination.
Delegate longer execution and research jobs, use nonblocking progress checks,
and avoid long blocking tool calls on the primary. User messages steer active
work; answer them promptly while delegated work continues. Small immediate
edits and decisions can remain with the primary when delegation would add
overhead.

**Owner requirement (2026-10-20), general across tasks:** long-running execution
must survive interruption or exit of the chat. Use an execution subagent or
background worker, with the actual host command detached from the chat/tool
process group, closed stdin, persistent logs and a durable completion receipt.
A background subagent alone does not establish process survival. Keep this chat
available; after reconnecting, reconcile the existing process and receipt rather
than rerunning creation or mutations. Preserve JEV Cargo routing, single-Cargo
exclusion and authorization boundaries; detachment grants no additional access.

For non-Cargo delegation, choose the appropriate agent role:

- `Explore` (fast read-only) for locating code, grepping symbols, answering "where is X."
- `Plan` for architecture and design before writing code.
- `general-purpose` only when the task needs multi-step reasoning or execution that Explore or Plan cannot cover.
- Use a more capable model for complex cross-crate reasoning, security review, or ambiguous architectural decisions, and for any standard edit, build fix, or test whose quality would drop on the low-cost agent.
- Do not spawn a subagent for a single-file edit or a direct grep you can do yourself.

Running read-only verification on git HEAD, active slots, MANIFEST header, file existence, mounts, and the October 27 log. Identity principals will be omitted from the API state. HANDOFF line 284 about whole-root is also being reviewed.

HANDOFF line 284 clarifies that activation must not require a reboot. Only directories and files actually used by the application deployment are relevant. The live script and mounts use per-path overlays rather than an overlay swap at `/opt/op-dbus/current`, which does not exist.

The 2026-10-14 text names `/opt/op-dbus/current` as the overlay swap point. Live mounts show nine separate targets and that path is absent. Jev should judge this conflict using the combined state. Both versions will be included. I am also checking for a later correction that the overlay is not a single symlink.

The activate-golden.sh comment about rotating read-only overlays at inventory host targets will be included as live script text. The MANIFEST will be read via sudo for the first 40 lines. Host paths and commit hashes are operational identifiers and will be sent to Jev. Identity principal UUIDs and session IDs remain excluded. Questions will reference paths by name.

Failure logs must not be mixed with deprecation questions. They could wrongly mark the current script as deprecated because of past failures. The plan is two separate requests. The first uses only owner documents and path existence on disk to classify paths and check if they are retired or the active command. The second request will handle relevance using failure facts.

The second request will pair deploy-failure facts with the user's core question: why a golden deploy of /srv/git/odbus-verified has not succeeded. Path documents must be excluded from this state to avoid pulling in deprecation judgments. The facts themselves need enough context for relevance decisions, such as noting that the slot design replaced /opt/op-dbus/current.

Request 2 will pair deploy-failure facts with owner notes that define success. Relevance is judged by whether the fact explains the deploy failure or its cause. The two requests can be sent in parallel because each carries its own independent state.

A single request is possible if path questions contain only path evidence and fact questions contain only failure facts. Shared context like the glossary belongs in state. But placing failure facts inside individual question instructions would hide them from path questions. This creates a conflict.

The skill confirms that each question is answered independently. A question sees only the shared state and its own instructions, not the instructions of other questions in the same request. This resolves the earlier concern about mixing path documents with failure facts in a single request.

A single request is sufficient. Shared owner documents and live path existence will go into the shared state. Failure facts will be placed only inside the relevance questions' instructions, not in state. Path questions will see only the procedure definitions and path evidence. Relevance questions will see both the procedure definitions and the failure facts.

Each relevance question will carry the full failure fact plus a direct prompt asking whether it explains the deploy failure. Because Jev sees only its own instructions and shared state, cross-fact sway is avoided. The skill requires that any context a question needs to answer must live inside that question's instructions.

Isolating relevance judgments would hide cross-fact dependencies. A single commit hash looks irrelevant without the full failure cluster. The skill warns that sharing facts across questions causes cross-sway. Two separate requests are therefore required.

Request A will contain only owner quotes and filesystem path existence. Request B will carry the full fact cluster plus a one-paragraph framing of the decision: which observed facts would change the explanation that the golden deploy has not succeeded. I am splitting the legacy activation path into two separate candidates to avoid using "or" in question subjects. The new stable identifiers are s6_service_manager, systemctl_shim, vendored_ui, ui_repo_direct, and send_receive.

Live verification corrected the prior summary. The op-release-launch comparison exited with code 2 because the files differ.

Re-running cmp showed the installed kit is byte-identical to this checkout for launch, boot, and bin. The prior hypothesis that activate-golden.sh would refuse was incorrect.

Exit code 2 from the prior comparison was an error, not a file difference. I will verify with cmp without the silent flag and checksums before reporting to Jev.

Slot B is mounted with 9 overlays and HANDOFF shows activation completed. The golden manifest hash matches the live slot hash, but the manifest was built from commit 380f692 while HANDOFF references commit b28a343. Catalog generation also differs: 228 versus 144. Both commits exist in odbus-verified.

odbus-verified HEAD is 2a6e40e, built at 04:13 on October 29. That predates the golden manifest build time of 22:27Z. The golden kit was built from odbus-rewrite rather than odbus-verified.

The active slot B overlay comes from a different source tree. Whether this counts as successful deployment depends on whether the user means this checkout.

An October 27 log entry shows an earlier activation failure that restored the previous state. This is historical context and does not explain the current mounted release.

The /opt/op-dbus/current symlink is absent. Live design uses per-target overlays rather than a whole-root swap.

deploy/runit/build-golden.sh is missing from the canonical repository but exists in the verified tree.

vendor/3tched-json-render-ui still exists in the repository, though AGENTS.md marks it retired for golden use.

The installed op-release binary is dated October 29, but its size matches the October 27 target/release build. The golden manifest lists binaries inside the golden tree, while the release kit is a separate launcher.

findmnt omitted the overlay source labels because it used OPTIONS instead of LABEL. The previous session had noted those labels as opdbus-release:b:release-640f40aa.

The awk filter searching for "opdbus-release" returned no matches. The findmnt output only shows /opt/emqx paths with lowerdir entries, so the overlay source labels were not present in that output.

The awk filter matched "opdbus-release" because the string appears in the lowerdir path `/var/lib/opdbus-release/base`, not in the LABEL column. The overlay source labels were likely empty.

I will run a tighter findmnt command to capture the overlay LABEL and SOURCE columns before reporting to Jev. I should not claim a specific label was present if it was not actually visible in this output. I also need to verify the relationship between commits 380f692, 2a6e40e, and b28a343.

I should also verify whether the golden manifest commit 380f692 is an ancestor of HEAD or on another branch. The corrected kit fact that the three files are byte-identical is a relevant negative fact to include, since it removes the previously suspected activation blocker. I did not re-verify directory modes or root ownership in activate-golden.sh, so I will only report what was actually checked.

The golden MANIFEST indicates the source repository is odbus-rewrite, whose HEAD is exactly 380f692. That commit exists in odbus-verified but remains ahead of its checked-out HEAD.

The handoff records head b28a343, which is older than both the current HEAD and the golden commit. Catalog generation numbers conflict: 144 in the handoff versus 228 in the manifest, though both share hash prefix 487402ba. This discrepancy matters for determining whether generation 144 describes the live golden. Kit files are byte-identical.

The prior comparison failure was stale. The identical kit files are not a cause of refusal. Leaving this fact out would introduce a false cause. Including it removes that false cause.

The byte-identical kit files are a negative finding. They rule out the kit-mismatch hypothesis as the cause of the failed deploy. This observation satisfies the criteria for ruling out a cause.

The October 27 failure is historical and likely superseded by the current mounted release. Its relevance to the present deploy is medium.

Path classification should distinguish whole-root from per-directory paths. The vendor directory still exists on disk even though notes mark it retired for golden use. Live existence must be recorded so Jev can compare documentation against actual host state.

For path questions, live existence matters alongside documentation. A path is only "right" if both the notes and the live host indicate it.

def noul(question, true, false, **fields):
    return {
        "type": "noul",
        "instructions": {"question": question, **fields},
        "criteria": {"true": true, "false": false},
    }


def path_questions():
    q = {}
    for key, desc in CANDIDATES:
        q[f"retired.{key}"] = noul(
            "Have the owner notes retired this candidate for golden deployment?",
            "A later note says not to use this candidate for a golden release.",
            "The newest note still includes this candidate in golden deployment.",
            candidate=desc,
        )
        q[f"command.{key}"] = noul(
            "Is this candidate the one command the newest note tells the operator to run?",
            "The newest note names this candidate as the one command to run.",
            "The newest note names a different command as the one to run.",
            candidate=desc,
        )
        q[f"step.{key}"] = noul(
            "Do the newest notes still include this candidate inside golden deployment?",
            "The newest notes say the deploy still does this.",
            "The newest notes leave this out of the deploy.",
            candidate=desc,
        )
        q[f"live.{key}"] = noul(
            "Is the active release on the host arranged this way right now?",
            "The mounted release matches this arrangement.",
            "The mounted release is arranged differently.",
            candidate=desc,
            live_host=LIVE,
        )
    return q


def fact_questions():
    q = {}
    for key, text in FACT_STATE["observations"].items():
        q[f"relevant.{key}"] = noul(
            "Would an account of whether this checkout's golden deploy has succeeded be wrong if it ignored this observation?",
            "Ignoring this observation would mis-state success or the cause.",
            "The account of that deploy stays the same when this observation is ignored.",
            observation=text,
        )
    return q


def post(state, questions, dest):
    payload = {"model": "jev-latest", "state": state, "questions": questions}
    with open(dest + ".request.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(payload, f)
    data = json.dumps(payload).encode()
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        URL,
        data=data,
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['TYPESAFE_API_KEY']}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        method="POST",
    )
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=180) as resp:
            body = resp.read()
            status = resp.status
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as exc:
        err = exc.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")[:2000]
        raise SystemExit(f"HTTP {exc.code} for {dest}: {err}") from exc
    parsed = json.loads(body)
    with open(dest + ".response.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(parsed, f)
    model = parsed.get("model")
    usage = parsed.get("usage")
    print(f"{dest}: HTTP {status} model {model} usage {usage} questions {len(questions)}")
    return parsed


def band(p):
    if p >= YES:
        return "yes"
    if p <= NO:
        return "no"
    return "unsettled"


def classify_path(retired, command, step, live):
    r, c, s, lv = band(retired), band(command), band(step), band(live)
    if "unsettled" in (r, c, s):
        label = "unsettled"
    elif r == "yes" and (c == "yes" or s == "yes"):
        label = "conflict"
    elif c == "yes" and r == "no":
        label = "current-command"
    elif s == "yes" and c == "no" and r == "no":
        label = "current-step"
    elif r == "yes" and c == "no" and s == "no":
        label = "deprecated"
    elif r == "no" and c == "no" and s == "no":
        label = "not-a-golden-path"
    else:
        label = "unsettled"
    return label, lv


def main():
    if not os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_API_KEY"):
        raise SystemExit("TYPESAFE_API_KEY is empty")
    paths = post(PATH_STATE, path_questions(), "/tmp/jev-paths")
    facts = post(FACT_STATE, fact_questions(), "/tmp/jev-facts")
    answers = paths["answers"]
    print("\nPATHS")
    for key, _desc in CANDIDATES:
        retired = answers[f"retired.{key}"]["noul"]
        command = answers[f"command.{key}"]["noul"]
        step = answers[f"step.{key}"]["noul"]
        live = answers[f"live.{key}"]["noul"]
        label, live_band = classify_path(retired, command, step, live)
        print(
            f"{key}\t{label}\tlive={live_band}\t"
            f"retired={retired:.3f}\tcommand={command:.3f}\tstep={step:.3f}\tlive={live:.3f}"
        )
    print("\nFACTS")
    for key in FACT_STATE["observations"]:
        p = facts["answers"][f"relevant.{key}"]["noul"]
        print(f"{key}\t{band(p)}\t{p:.3f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The journal is an interrupted deploy.

Only stale kit copies will be removed. The installed kit and all active snapshots will remain untouched. Old directories and binaries that do not match the current release hash will be deleted.

Four stale directories will be deleted: activation-prep, bootstrap-20261018, host-fuse-split, and bootstrap-20261023. The last contains only old and new kit pairs.

The live kit is the one in `/usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release`. The other copies are older binaries from October 18–23, unused by the mounts. I am removing those and leaving the active slot, the rollback slot, and the unfinished journal alone.

sudo -n bash -c '
set -eu
keep_rel=2fa4b27914c35fc7b623c424c866536335cf5ce58fca01019c4c5616b1fdc205
# Refuse to run if the installed kit is not the known working trio.
got=$(sha256sum /usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release/op-release | awk "{print \$1}")
[ "$got" = "$keep_rel" ]
dirs='
/var/lib/opdbus-release/kit-backup-20261018T134200Z
/var/lib/opdbus-release/provision-kit-20261018.ahFxfCuC
/var/lib/opdbus-release/readiness-kit-20261023-QVdJko
/var/lib/opdbus-release/bootstrap-20261023-6etb9N
/var/lib/opdbus-release/activation-prep-20261018T162600Z/kit
/var/lib/opdbus-release/activation-prep-20261018T162600Z/controller-directory-mode
'
for d in $dirs; do
  [ -d "$d" ]
  # Every op-release in here must differ from the installed one.
  find "$d" -type f -name "op-release*" | while read -r f; do
    case "$f" in
      *op-release-launch|*op-release-activate) continue ;;
    esac
    h=$(sha256sum "$f" | awk "{print \$1}")
    if [ "$h" = "$keep_rel" ]; then
      echo "REFUSING $f matches installed kit" >&2
      exit 1
    fi
  done
done
rm -rf -- $dirs
rm -f -- \
  /var/lib/opdbus-release/bootstrap-20261018.sYDTwX/op-release.before-same-parent-20261018 \
  /var/lib/opdbus-release/bootstrap-20261018.sYDTwX/manifest.before-same-parent-20261018.sha256 \

echo REMOVED
echo "=== remaining op-release binaries under release state ==="

echo "=== installed ==="
sha256sum /usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release/op-release /usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release/op-release-launch /etc/init.d/op-release-activate
echo "=== overlays ==="
findmnt -t overlay -n -o TARGET,LABEL | awk "index(\$0,\"opdbus-release:b\")"
'

This is a clear architecture request.

The failure mode is now clear. etched0 is meant for the subsidiary to access the rest of the system, not the chatbot root. The chatbot must provision a clone inside the subsidiary. The hackathon is gated by etched0 with only internet access and no 3tched networking. Every method is accessed through fusefs.

The current hackathon mount likely uses the host chatbot identity directly instead of a clone. etched0 is down and has no address. I need to read SUBSIDIARY-SLED.md and network.md before provisioning. The root chatbot fused with the WG server key becomes the control plane. Linux users become subsidiaries. The old chatbot key maps to the 3tched container as subsidiary root.

The hackathon subsidiary was started with Linux user 3tched and a 3tchedfs mount of identity b0c777e3. This appears to be the same root chatbot identity rather than a clone. The contradiction between etched0 being needed for subsidiary access and the restriction that no 3tched networking is allowed remains unresolved.

1→# Subsidiaries and the identity sled

How an identity works as the embodiment of a subsidiary. Marked **existing**
(in 3tched today), **proven** (demonstrated 2026-10-28) or **planned**.

## Hierarchy (owner model)

- **Root**: the 3tched control plane — the only root on the system. Its chatbot is a one-off part of the
  system core, to be fused with the WireGuard server key so it can never be a
10→  peer (session `<root-session>`). **Planned** — no
  supported re-key operation yet.
- **Root has no execution rights**: it holds authority but executes nothing
  itself; execution is delegated through the execution tracker. A human acting
  as root needs **two approvals** (two-person rule). Today `elevation` offers a
  single-use ticket (`authorize_task`, 60 s TTL); the second approval is new
  work. **Planned.**
- **Owner override** (owner requirement): while the owner is the only human,
  his identity must be able to override the two-approval rule. Proposed:
  routine root actions take two approvals from two independent owner devices
20→  (session + hardware key/phone); an override is break-glass — fresh
  hardware-key confirmation, a cancellable delay, a receipt anchored on-chain,
  and a notification on a second channel — so even the owner cannot act as
  root silently. A designated human second approver replaces this later.
  **Planned.**
- **Second approver = the control-plane chatbot** (owner decision): it co-signs
  the owner's root actions **by policy, not persuasion** — it receives only a
  structured request (operation, resource, identity, applicable policy), never
  free-text justification; atomic judgments (the chatbot or Jev) feed code that
  decides approve/refuse; anything outside written policy is refused and only
30→  break-glass can override; every decision is receipted with its reasons. It
  approves but never executes. Tiers: routine = owner + chatbot within policy;
  out of policy = refused, break-glass only; later = human second approver.
  **Planned.**
- **Subsidiaries**: Linux users on the system. Each subsidiary is bounded by
  its home directory. **Planned.**
- **Hackathon subsidiary**: embodied by identity `<subsidiary-session>` (today's
  `3tchedCtlChatbot`). **Existing.**

## What the sled is (existing)
40→
The sled is the identity. For each identity session it holds:

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| Record | session id, WireGuard public key, principal kind, genesis hash, trace id, schema version, active flag, timestamps |
| Instance binding | the container that embodies it (name, native UUID, pool) |
| Private leaf | the identity's writable storage, with the canonical subvolumes `@agent_soul`, `@agent_memory`, `@agent_rules`, `@agent_skills`, `@agent_user`, `@agent_shared` (shared/soul read-only; memory/rules/skills/user writable) |
| Session ledger | session events and receipts; the input for vectorization |

50→Session and principal ids are derived from the public key
(`op-identity::session::derive_session_id` / `derive_principal_id`, Blake3
KDF), so the key, genesis and chain *are* the identity — not a machine.

Lifecycle rules (existing): the identity subsystem owns minting; Cozo owns
assignment; login/start/stop never add or remove Btrfs members; the bridge
only verifies externally mounted storage. Never edit sled rows directly.

## How a subsidiary acts

60→1. The subsidiary's identity runs in its own container with a 3tchedFS mount
   (lungs). **Proven** for `<subsidiary-session>`.
2. On the host, the same identity's mount is exposed inside the
   subsidiary's home, e.g. `/home/<user>/<Subsidiary>/3tchedfs` and
   `/home/<user>/<Subsidiary>/threetched`, bound to that session
   (`--lungs-session`) with call files owned by that Linux user only
   (call-owner UID). Other users can read schemas but cannot act. **Planned.**
3. Every call: kernel or credential identifies the identity → bridge checks the
   exact capability → MutationEngine commits → receipt. **Proven.**
4. threetched (model/agent) operations used by a subsidiary are its own:
70→   one router agent per subsidiary with its own model, tool set and budget
   (`max_actions_per_hour`, `max_cost_per_day_cents`). **Planned.**

## Sled + execution tracker (planned)

Every tool call is validated by the one shared execution tracker and written
to the identity's sled session ledger; that ledger is vectorized (Qdrant) so
the identity can answer questions about its own history. Code: branch
`recover/execution-tracker` (`identity_sled_dispatch::subscribe_execution_tracker`).

80→## Sled + Web3 (planned)

- The index's first entry for an identity records its origin (3tched origin
  session, genesis) and is anchored on-chain.
- A secp256k1 wallet is bound to the identity by a signed link recorded in
  its sled and in the index (the WireGuard key is X25519 and cannot sign
  Ethereum transactions).
- Each index entry references the receipt (`operation_id`, `event_hash`) that
  authorised it.

90→## Sled + OSCAL boundaries (planned)

The subsidiary's OSCAL profile compiles into: the identity's capability grants
(what it may call), router budgets (how much), and OpenFlow policy on its
network (where it may connect). The bridge already enforces grants on every
call; the new work is generating them from OSCAL.

## Sled + execution tracker (planned)

Every tool call is validated by the one shared execution tracker and written
to the identity's sled session ledger; that ledger is vectorized (Qdrant) so
the identity can answer questions about its own history. Code: branch
`recover/execution-tracker` (`identity_sled_dispatch::subscribe_execution_tracker`).

## Sled + Web3 (planned)

- The index's first entry for an identity records its origin (3tched origin
  session, genesis) and is anchored on-chain.
- A secp256k1 wallet is bound to the identity by a signed link recorded in
  its sled and in the index (the WireGuard key is X25519 and cannot sign
  Ethereum transactions).
- Each index entry references the receipt (`operation_id`, `event_hash`) that
  authorised it.

## Sled + OSCAL boundaries (planned)

The subsidiary's OSCAL profile compiles into: the identity's capability grants
(what it may call), router budgets (how much), and OpenFlow policy on its
network (where it may connect). The bridge already enforces grants on every
call; the new work is generating them from OSCAL.

# Incus: configuration first, storage-driver ownership

20→Project-local skill authored from the official Incus documentation below;
not an imported third-party skill or a container-sandbox wrapper. Documentation
review is not proof that any example has been applied to this host. Check the
installed client/server version and applicable API extensions before using
version-dependent options.

## Start with the actual declaration

An Incus instance is configured through instance properties, `config`,
`devices` and ordered `profiles`. The CLI exposes this as YAML; do not invent
30→a separate authoritative YAML file on disk. Incus owns its configuration.

Read both local and expanded instance configuration. Later profiles override
earlier ones; instance-local configuration overrides profiles. Editing a
shared profile affects every instance that uses it. Do not use expanded
configuration as a blind replacement: it flattens inherited settings.

Read-only infrastructure diagnostics, within the assigned maintenance scope:

```sh
40→incus version
incus config show <instance>
incus config show <instance> --expanded
incus profile show <profile>
incus storage show <pool>
incus storage volume list <pool>
incus storage volume show <pool> container/<instance>
```

Confirm the selected remote, project, instance type, native UUID and stopped
50→or running state. A name alone is not an identity or authorization proof.
Use `--force-local` only when explicitly diagnosing this host's local daemon.

## Declare native disks under devices

Example fragment for a NEW container's root on an existing Btrfs pool named
`3tched` (not a migration instruction for an existing container):

```yaml
devices:
60→  root:
    type: disk
    pool: 3tched
    path: /
```

Incus creates the instance's root storage volume at instance creation. Its
Btrfs driver uses a subvolume for a container filesystem volume. Do not
manually create a per-container `.img`, GPT, `losetup` mapping or filesystem
as an assumed prerequisite for this native root declaration.
70→
Additional managed filesystem volumes are separate objects. Create the
custom volume through the supported control plane first; its device then
names the pool, volume and guest mount path:

```yaml
devices:
  data:
    type: disk
    pool: 3tched
80→    source: identity-data
    path: /data
```

This references an existing custom filesystem volume named `identity-data`;
it does not create that volume. Custom volumes persist independently of the
instance until explicitly deleted. Do not casually share identity-private
volumes. A device with a host-path `source` and no pool is a host-backed
mount, not an Incus-managed custom volume.

90→For standalone Incus administration, the native commands are
`incus storage volume create <pool> <volume>` (filesystem by default),
`incus storage volume attach <pool> <volume> <instance> <device> <guest-path>`
and `incus config device add <instance> <device> disk pool=<pool> source=<volume> path=<guest-path>`.
These are reference syntax, NOT permission to bypass this repository's
identity-bound provisioning operations. Do not replay them against an
already provisioned identity without the authorized maintenance contract.

## Do not conflate these layers

100→| Object | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Btrfs pool backing | Existing block device, loop file or Btrfs subvolume; inspect the pool's `source`. |
| Container filesystem volume | Managed filesystem tree; Btrfs driver represents it as a subvolume. No additional loop per volume is needed. |
| Container `type: disk` device | Mount inside the container, not a VM-style emulated partitioned disk. A host block source is mounted, not automatically passed through as guest block hardware. |
| Custom `block` or `iso` volume | Attachable to VMs, not containers. Do not switch instance type to work around this restriction. |
| Btrfs VM disk | Incus uses a backing file because Btrfs does not natively provide block volumes. This is not the container-volume model. |
| Btrfs seeding/sprouting | Separate block-device filesystem operation; a subvolume is not a writable block member for `btrfs device add`. |

A loop backing an entire existing Incus pool does not imply a loop for each
110→container. Never detach an existing pool backing to satisfy a statement that
container subvolumes need no loops. Do not create new loop-backed pools or
per-container raw images unless that distinct layout is explicitly requested.

An Incus root declaration alone does NOT implement an external immutable
seed plus writable Btrfs member, a GPT two-partition upgrade replica, or a
read-only overlay. Name any conflict between such requirements and native
filesystem volumes before changing the design. Do not silently replace
seeding with copied roots, snapshots, or an OverlayFS provisioning fallback.
Use the `btrfs` skill for actual seed, membership and send/receive mechanics;
120→Incus owns its managed-volume lifecycle.

## Preserve ownership, lifecycle and admission

- Begin repository operations in the assigned identity's mounted 3tchedFS.
  Discover declared operations and arguments there. Preserve principal,
  session, grants and Cozo identity-to-storage binding. Missing admission is
  not permission to use the local Incus socket or edit Cozo directly.
- Inspect current native configuration and the provisioning owner before
  changing an existing root. Changing the `pool` key is not a storage migration.
130→  Preserve native UUID, session/key binding, mount ownership and receipts.
- Keep containers unprivileged, their UID/GID mapping, storage ioctl denials
  and existing device allowlist. Do not grant guest block administration,
  nesting, unrestricted host paths or daemon sockets to make storage work.
- Explicit creation may establish approved storage once. Login, boot, start,
  stop, restart, logout and recovery must not allocate new identity leaves
  or add/remove Btrfs members. Restore/verify existing storage instead.
- Do not mutate Incus-owned storage directories or live overlay lower layers
  behind the daemon. Host storage maintenance must use its supported owner,
  exact device/FSID/mount checks and explicit authorized scope.
140→- Before any receive, verify the intended mounted destination and its FSID;
  an existing directory is insufficient. Never receive into a fallback path
  on the host root filesystem when the intended mount is missing.
- Distinguish source configuration, accepted operation, native state and
  deployed readiness. Report the operation receipt and authoritative result;
  no claim of success from writing YAML alone. Do not auto-start containers,
  change service managers or run test suites merely to install this skill.

## 3tched Ubuntu provisioning contract

150→- Use Ubuntu 26.04 LTS (Resolute Raccoon) inside the container. This does not
  change the host's distribution or service manager.
- Reuse the initialized 3tched Ubuntu seed contents, including when the owner
  explicitly selects different backing storage. A generic Ubuntu root archive
  may initialize a new seed only; never use a generic image as a later
  container-root fallback. Never modify a sealed seed with retained dependents.
- Compose each root from that seed through the existing host storage owner.
  Preserve existing 3tched integrations and network declarations; install only
  demonstrated container runtime dependencies.
- Keep persistent CozoDB data on the approved identity-owned writable storage.
160→  Do not force a separate Cozo subvolume through `btrfs device add`: that
  operation applies only when the selected design actually adds a block member.
  An Incus filesystem subvolume is not a block-device operand. Require the
  exact approved device before adding it; do not infer permission to allocate
  a raw image, loop, LV or replacement disk.
- For an explicitly approved partitioned seed image, a host `losetup
  --find --show --partscan IMAGE` mapping exposes partition devices such as
  `/dev/loopNp1` and `/dev/loopNp2`; separate loop allocations per partition
  are not inherently required. Finalize and unmount the root filesystem before
  setting `btrfstune -S 1` on partition 1 only. Check the existing SEEDING flag
170→  and skip an already sealed base; never retune on login/start/reboot. The flag
  persists in the image, while kernel mappings must be restored after reboot.
  Protect only the base partition read-only, not the whole image when partition
  2 must remain writable. Never set SEEDING on the upgrade receive filesystem.
- Distinguish an immutable base partition from a writable upgrade receiver.
  Keep the receiver filesystem/parent writable for `btrfs receive`, while
  preserving received snapshots and common incremental baselines read-only.
  Receive a new version into the parent, not over an existing `@upgrade`;
  publish it only through the host-owned overlay lifecycle, without modifying
  an in-use lower tree. Track each container's receiver and baseline explicitly;
180→  do not infer a shared mutable receiver from a shared image/template name.
- When the owner explicitly requests a raw leaf image under the Cozo store,
  first locate the live store through supported metadata or open-path evidence;
  do not create a duplicate database or read private records to find its path.
  Put image files outside RocksDB `data`, use a private directory and exclusive
  creation, and retain the exact size/inode/operation result. A created image
  does not establish Btrfs membership or migrate Cozo data into that image.
- Distinguish direct regular-file rejection from a provisioning-policy denial.
  Installed btrfs-progs may reject a regular `.img` with `is not a block device`;
  report that real result rather than claiming completion or silently creating
190→  a loop/device-mapper alternative against the owner's instruction. Full
  allocation does not change a regular file's type: if a nonsparse retry is
  explicitly requested, verify allocated bytes (disable compression on the
  empty file before writing zeros), and do not repeat that allocation after
  the same type rejection.
- Reconcile matching creation receipts and verify the retained storage binding
  on repeats. Normal lifecycle operations must not repeat device-add, format
  storage or recreate roots. Interrupted intent requires reconciliation, not
  an automatic new allocation.
- Reuse existing identity, authorization and policy services. Do not build
200→  parallel services, mint new credentials, broaden grants or edit Cozo
  directly as part of OS provisioning. Verify the mounted filesystem and
  authoritative binding before claiming persistence is configured.

## Official references

Consult the version matching the installed daemon where behavior differs.
These upstream pages were reviewed for this skill on 2026-10-19:

- [Instance configuration](https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/docs/main/explanation/instance_config/)
210→- [Profiles and inheritance](https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/docs/main/profiles/)
- [Disk devices](https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/docs/main/reference/devices_disk/)
- [Btrfs storage driver](https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/docs/main/reference/storage_btrfs/)
- [Storage volume creation, attachment and content-type restrictions](https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/docs/main/howto/storage_volumes/)

Description:
  Copy instances within or in between servers

  Transfer modes (--mode):
   - pull: Target server pulls the data from the source server (source must listen on network)
   - push: Source server pushes the data to the target server (target must listen on network)
   - relay: The CLI connects to both source and server and proxies the data (both source and target must listen on network)

  The pull transfer mode is the default as it is compatible with all server versions.

  -d, --device                  New key/value to apply to a specific device
  -e, --ephemeral               Ephemeral instance
      --instance-only           Copy the instance without its snapshots

content.text:
Session ID is cc59ab57-d94a-8334-222b-8077ef033320.

Copying the container now. The new instance will receive a fresh public key via config override. The original key won't be echoed to tool output.

The public key will be included in the final response since it is part of the identity. The private key will remain hidden. The copy command uses a long timeout and immediate detach persistence.

The copy command applies the new display name, WireGuard public key, session ID, and UTS hostname. After creation it removes the persistent device and clears the original creation metadata.

The private key is pushed into the new container with strict permissions. A bridged network device is attached to it. The source container is verified to still hold the original public key and persistence. The clone is checked to confirm its public key differs, has no persistence, and uses the correct display name. The host copy of the private key will be shred after the push succeeds.

Temporary derive files will be removed once the session and public key are recorded. The copy timeout is set to ten minutes, with polling if it exceeds that. Proceeding with the copy of the running container.

rawInput.command:
set -eu
PUB=$(cat /tmp/etched-hackathon.pub)
SID=$(cat /tmp/etched-hackathon.sid)
sudo -n incus copy 3tchedCtlChatbot etched-hackathon --instance-only \
  -c user.display_name='etched::hackathon' \
  -c "user.opdbus.wireguard_public_key=${PUB}" \
  -c "user.opdbus.session_id=${SID}" \
  -c "raw.lxc=lxc.uts.name = ${SID}"
echo COPY_DONE
sudo -n incus config device remove etched-hackathon persist
sudo -n incus config unset etched-hackathon user.opdbus.creation_digest || true
sudo -n incus config unset etched-hackathon user.opdbus.creation_operation || true
sudo -n incus file push --mode 600 --uid 0 --gid 0 /tmp/etched-hackathon.key etched-hackathon/root/etched-hackathon.key
if sudo -n incus config device add etched-hackathon eth0 nic nictype=bridged parent=etched0; then
  echo NIC_OK
else
  echo NIC_FAILED
fi
echo '=== source ==='
sudo -n incus list 3tchedCtlChatbot -c ns,status -f csv
sudo -n incus config get 3tchedCtlChatbot user.opdbus.session_id
sudo -n incus config device get 3tchedCtlChatbot persist source
echo '=== clone ==='
sudo -n incus list etched-hackathon -c ns,status -f csv
sudo -n incus config get etched-hackathon user.display_name
sudo -n incus config get etched-hackathon user.opdbus.session_id
sudo -n incus config get etched-hackathon user.opdbus.wireguard_public_key
sudo -n incus config show etched-hackathon | awk '/^devices:/{p=1} p&&/^[^ ]/{if(!seen++)next} p'
echo '=== persist on clone? ==='
sudo -n incus config device show etched-hackathon
shred -u /tmp/etched-hackathon.key
rm -f /tmp/derive_sid.rs
rm -rf /tmp/derive-sid
echo HOST_KEY_REMOVED

The public key was printed in the tool output.

The private key was shred from the host and now lives only in the container. I will verify that the public key in config is not the root's, that etched0 still has no IP and fail_mode secure, that the clone has no IPv4, that the source session remains active, that the host key file is gone, and that the FUSE mount stays on the root session.

The clone is not a sled identity, so the hackathon FUSE mount was not pointed at it. Live subsidiary methods still use the root session. The NIC was added while stopped, so the veth likely does not appear on etched0 until start. I will verify that etched0 remains down and no new ports appear while stopped. The root public key is unchanged. The device show output is clean.

The clone public key is confirmed different from the root key. The container will remain stopped. Leftover files in /tmp will be deleted. I am checking how to verify the file mode inside the stopped container.

The key file inside the container is mode 600 and owned by root. I will check the OVS port list for etched0 to confirm no port was added while the container was stopped.

I did not rebind the FUSE mount to the clone because the sealed provision path rejects new keys. Pointing the live mount at the new session would cause every hackathon call to fail admission. The clone remains stopped and gated to etched0.

The clone is not a sled identity. etched0 has no uplink and fail_mode secure drops traffic, so the container cannot reach 3tched or the internet until flows and an uplink exist. I will not add those with ovs-vsctl because of the standing prohibition, and openflow.write is withheld.

list-ports returned empty, though ovs-vsctl show previously listed etched0 as an internal interface.

The bridge's internal port is absent from list-ports, which is expected. The pub and sid files were removed after the listing. The clone's public key was present in the previous tool output and will be reported as the identity label.

`etched::hackathon` is a stopped copy of the chatbot with its own key. The sealed identity path cannot assign that key, so this is the container copy you allowed.

The bridge refuses `provision_container` for a new key. It will not compose or copy an identity root, and a new public key has to already be a registered principal. The root chatbot is unchanged: `3tchedCtlChatbot` is still running as session `b0c777e3-0955-cd8b-3d01-ca12998cae28` and still owns its persist volume.

The clone:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Incus name | `etched-hackathon` |
| Display name | `etched::hackathon` |
| Session | `cc59ab57-d94a-8334-222b-8077ef033320` |
| Public key | `Wycws7Udq0XTSN7I45JPP+CL9ZS4MxhXlhM4zAn8FX0=` |
| Private key | `/root/etched-hackathon.key` inside the container, mode 600. The host copy was removed. |
| State | Stopped |
| NIC | `eth0` on `etched0` only |
| Disk | Its own root volume. The root chatbot's persist volume was removed from the copy. |
| Profile | `3tched-lungs`, so a future start can see the FUSE socket |

`etched0` is still down, with no address and no extra ports. Fail-mode is secure, so this NIC has no path to 3tched and no internet until that bridge has an uplink and flows. Nothing was added to `ovsbr0` or `hackbr0`.

The hackathon FUSE mount at `/home/3tched/Hackathon/3tchedfs` still uses the root session. Pointing it at `cc59ab57-…` now would fail admission, because this key is not in the identity sled. The container is not a second root.

1→# Subsidiaries and the identity sled

How an identity works as the embodiment of a subsidiary. Marked **existing**
(in 3tched today), **proven** (demonstrated 2026-10-28) or **planned**.

## Hierarchy (owner model)

- **Root**: the 3tched control plane — the only root on the system. Its chatbot is a one-off part of the
  system core, to be fused with the WireGuard server key so it can never be a
10→  peer (session `<root-session>`). **Planned** — no
  supported re-key operation yet.
- **Root has no execution rights**: it holds authority but executes nothing
  itself; execution is delegated through the execution tracker. A human acting
  as root needs **two approvals** (two-person rule). Today `elevation` offers a
  single-use ticket (`authorize_task`, 60 s TTL); the second approval is new
  work. **Planned.**
- **Owner override** (owner requirement): while the owner is the only human,
  his identity must be able to override the two-approval rule. Proposed:
  routine root actions take two approvals from two independent owner devices
20→  (session + hardware key/phone); an override is break-glass — fresh
  hardware-key confirmation, a cancellable delay, a receipt anchored on-chain,
  and a notification on a second channel — so even the owner cannot act as
  root silently. A designated human second approver replaces this later.
  **Planned.**
- **Second approver = the control-plane chatbot** (owner decision): it co-signs
  the owner's root actions **by policy, not persuasion** — it receives only a
  structured request (operation, resource, identity, applicable policy), never
  free-text justification; atomic judgments (the chatbot or Jev) feed code that
  decides approve/refuse; anything outside written policy is refused and only
30→  break-glass can override; every decision is receipted with its reasons. It
  approves but never executes. Tiers: routine = owner + chatbot within policy;
  out of policy = refused, break-glass only; later = human second approver.
  **Planned.**
- **Subsidiaries**: Linux users on the system. Each subsidiary is bounded by
  its home directory. **Planned.**
- **Hackathon subsidiary**: embodied by identity `<subsidiary-session>` (today's
  `3tchedCtlChatbot`). **Existing.**

## What the sled is (existing)
40→
The sled is the identity. For each identity session it holds:

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| Record | session id, WireGuard public key, principal kind, genesis hash, trace id, schema version, active flag, timestamps |
| Instance binding | the container that embodies it (name, native UUID, pool) |
| Private leaf | the identity's writable storage, with the canonical subvolumes `@agent_soul`, `@agent_memory`, `@agent_rules`, `@agent_skills`, `@agent_user`, `@agent_shared` (shared/soul read-only; memory/rules/skills/user writable) |
| Session ledger | session events and receipts; the input for vectorization |

50→Session and principal ids are derived from the public key
(`op-identity::session::derive_session_id` / `derive_principal_id`, Blake3
KDF), so the key, genesis and chain *are* the identity — not a machine.

Lifecycle rules (existing): the identity subsystem owns minting; Cozo owns
assignment; login/start/stop never add or remove Btrfs members; the bridge
only verifies externally mounted storage. Never edit sled rows directly.

## How a subsidiary acts

60→1. The subsidiary's identity runs in its own container with a 3tchedFS mount
   (lungs). **Proven** for `<subsidiary-session>`.
2. On the host, the same identity's mount is exposed inside the
   subsidiary's home, e.g. `/home/<user>/<Subsidiary>/3tchedfs` and
   `/home/<user>/<Subsidiary>/threetched`, bound to that session
   (`--lungs-session`) with call files owned by that Linux user only
   (call-owner UID). Other users can read schemas but cannot act. **Planned.**
3. Every call: kernel or credential identifies the identity → bridge checks the
   exact capability → MutationEngine commits → receipt. **Proven.**
4. threetched (model/agent) operations used by a subsidiary are its own:
70→   one router agent per subsidiary with its own model, tool set and budget
   (`max_actions_per_hour`, `max_cost_per_day_cents`). **Planned.**

## Sled + execution tracker (planned)

Every tool call is validated by the one shared execution tracker and written
to the identity's sled session ledger; that ledger is vectorized (Qdrant) so
the identity can answer questions about its own history. Code: branch
`recover/execution-tracker` (`identity_sled_dispatch::subscribe_execution_tracker`).

80→## Sled + Web3 (planned)

content.text:
1→# Etched in Schema — brief for Muse Spark

Hackathon: Meta Model API, **Startup Track — judged on a working product**.
Builder: Jeremy Hobson (3tched).

**Scope (owner, 2026-10-28):** the identity/3tched platform predates the
hackathon and is used through its interfaces. The new, judged development is
(1) compliance routing, (2) rule enforcement, (3) policy, and (4) a drop-in
consumer app (team chat first). The UI is optional. See README "Goals" for the
10→golden path. Sections below about the avatar, CMS demo and on-chain anchoring
are background, not the critical path.
State as of 2026-10-28. Everything marked **proven** was demonstrated on the
host that day; everything else is planned.

## The project in one paragraph

A self-contained 3tched identity — the "twin", the living embodiment of a
3tched subsidiary — turns a business goal into deployed, verified
infrastructure. It acts only through its own typed filesystem (3tchedFS),
20→every action is authorised against its capabilities and leaves a
tamper-evident receipt, and a Web3 index anchored on-chain lets anyone verify
who did what, under what authority, without trusting the agent or operator.
That link between on-chain artifacts and accountable, authorised actors is the
gap blocking Web3 adoption.

## Proven today

- **Identity container**: `3tchedCtlChatbot` (Incus, pool `3tched`, profile
  `3tched-lungs`), identity session `<subsidiary-session>`,
30→  service principal, persist volume, kept running by runit `chatbot-identity`.

# etched::hackathon — what to do before going further

Owner direction, 2026-10-30. The chatbot is the root of this system. The
hackathon subsidiary is a clone of that chatbot, named `etched::hackathon`.
The clone is gated on `etched0`, with internet only and no network path to
3tched. Every method is a file on its 3tchedFS mount.

One repo comes first. Do not register the clone, start it, or retarget the
mount until that consolidation is the tree you mean to keep. This file is the
piece that goes in first.

Checked on the host 2026-10-30. **Proven** means a command showed it that day.
**Planned** means the owner still has to do it.

## What you need to do

1. Finish bringing the trees into the one repo. Leave the clone stopped while
   you do that.
2. Make `etched::hackathon` a real identity. The bridge will not do this.
   `provision_container` stops with: prepare the shared physical seed, the
   private writable leaf, and the container outside the bridge; the bridge
   cannot compose, mount, or copy an identity root. A new public key is
   accepted only when it is already an active registered principal. Register
   public key `Wycws7Udq0XTSN7I45JPP+CL9ZS4MxhXlhM4zAn8FX0=`, then run the
   external seed provision so the sled binds session
   `cc59ab57-d94a-8334-222b-8077ef033320` to Incus instance `etched-hackathon`.
   Do not edit sled or Cozo rows by hand. Do not add a Btrfs member from
   login or start.
3. Prove the binding. A `get_own_identity` call on a mount whose
   `--lungs-session` is `cc59ab57-d94a-8334-222b-8077ef033320` must return that
   session. Until it does, leave `/etc/sv/subsidiary-hackathon-3tchedfs/run`
   on the root session `b0c777e3-0955-cd8b-3d01-ca12998cae28`.
4. After that proof, change `SESSION=` in that run script to the clone
   session and restart `subsidiary-hackathon-3tchedfs`. A call as Linux user
   `3tched` through `/home/3tched/Hackathon/3tchedfs` must then return the
   clone session.
5. Internet on `etched0` is a later step. The bridge is down, fail-mode
   `secure`, with no address and no uplink, so the clone's NIC cannot reach
   3tched and cannot reach the internet. Do not rebuild `etched0` with
   `ovs-vsctl` (the 2026-10-28 correction in
   `docs/src/operations/network.md`). `openflow.write` stays withheld until
   enforcement refuses a flow on any bridge other than `etched0`. Do not put
   the old `hackbr0` NIC back on the root chatbot.

Leave the root chatbot as `3tchedCtlChatbot`, session
`b0c777e3-0955-cd8b-3d01-ca12998cae28`. It is the root, not the subsidiary.

## New

New on 2026-10-30, because the sealed identity path cannot assign the key:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Display name | `etched::hackathon` |
| Incus name | `etched-hackathon` (a name cannot contain `::`) |
| State | Stopped. **Proven.** |
| Session | `cc59ab57-d94a-8334-222b-8077ef033320`, Blake3 `derive_session_id` of the new public key |
| Public key | `Wycws7Udq0XTSN7I45JPP+CL9ZS4MxhXlhM4zAn8FX0=` |
| Private key | `/root/etched-hackathon.key` inside the container, mode 600, root. The host copy was removed. |
| Disk | Its own root volume on pool `3tched`. The root chatbot's persist volume is not attached. |
| Profile | `3tched-lungs`, so a later start can see the lungs socket |
| NIC | `eth0`, bridged, parent `etched0` only. Not `ovsbr0`, not `hackbr0`. |
| Sled | Not registered. This container is not yet an identity. |

The container is a wholesale copy of `3tchedCtlChatbot` with the name and
keys changed. It is not a seed provision and it is not a second root.

## Old and existing

These were already on the host. They were not replaced.

| Item | What it still is |
|---|---|
| Root chatbot | `3tchedCtlChatbot`, running, display name `control-plane-chatbot`, session `b0c777e3-0955-cd8b-3d01-ca12998cae28`, public key `Env5zPMmM1Zhypu5/DY/yU4PRYW/4AOEq2KZ4OSc+18=`, persist volume `3tchedCtlChatbot-persist`. **Proven** still running after the copy. |
| Hackathon mount | `/home/3tched/Hackathon/3tchedfs`, runit `subsidiary-hackathon-3tchedfs`, Linux user `3tched` (uid 1001). **Proven** mounted. `SESSION=` is still the root session. |
| `etched0` | OVS bridge, fail-mode `secure`, no address, no uplink, no extra ports. Created 2026-10-28 with `ovs-vsctl`, so it has no identity and no receipt. |
| `hackbr0` | The 2026-10-28 internet-only Incus bridge. It is down. Its NIC is not on the root container and not on the clone. |
| Other instances | `3tched-container` and `chatbot-template-sysprep` are stopped. `qdrant-recovered` is running. None of them is the subsidiary. |
| Identity rule | The sled is the identity. Session id is derived from the public key. The bridge verifies storage; it does not compose a root. |

The 2026-10-28 docs said the hackathon subsidiary *was* `3tchedCtlChatbot`.
That sentence described the mount that is still live. It is not the owner
model as of 2026-10-30.

## What changed in the old

Brought forward only far enough for the clone to exist beside the root.
Nothing below re-keyed the root or moved the live mount.

| Old thing | Change on 2026-10-30 |
|---|---|
| `3tchedCtlChatbot` | Copied to `etched-hackathon` with `incus copy --instance-only`. The source was left running, on the same session, with the same public key and the same persist volume. |
| Copy's inherited identity labels | Display name, public key, session id, and `lxc.uts.name` set to the clone. `user.opdbus.creation_digest` and `user.opdbus.creation_operation` unset so the copy does not claim the root's creation receipt. |
| Copy's `persist` device | Removed, so the clone does not mount `3tchedCtlChatbot-persist`. |
| `etched0` | The bridge was not edited. The clone's Incus NIC names it as parent. While the clone is stopped, `etched0` still has no extra ports. |
| Hackathon run script and mount | Unchanged. Calls as `3tched` are still the root chatbot. |
| `docs/SUBSIDIARY-SLED.md`, `docs/RUNTIME.md`, `docs/DEV-CYCLE.md` | The old "the subsidiary is the root container" lines now point here. |
| `docs/src/operations/network.md` | A 2026-10-30 note records the clone NIC. The 2026-10-28 `etched0` and `hackbr0` notes stay as history. |

## Also on the host, not the subsidiary

Stale release-kit copies from 2026-10-18 and 2026-10-23 were removed because
their `op-release` binaries did not match the installed kit. The installed
kit that remains is `/usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release/op-release`,
`op-release-launch`, and `/etc/init.d/op-release-activate`, with
`manifest.sha256` matching those three. Slot B
`release-640f40aa-7b7a-446e-a614-3aecb7771d90` was left mounted. The
unfinished journal at `quiescent-delete:489` for candidate
`release-97d42309-3d63-4227-ac48-23f492466652` was left in `slots.json`.
That journal is not this subsidiary.

# etched::hackathon — what to do before going further

Owner direction, 2026-10-30. The chatbot is the root of this system. The
hackathon subsidiary is a clone of that chatbot, named `etched::hackathon`.
The clone is gated on `etched0`, with internet only and no network path to
3tched. Every method is a file on its 3tchedFS mount.

One repo comes first. Do not register the clone, start it, or retarget the
mount until that consolidation is the tree you mean to keep. This file is the
piece that goes in first.

Checked on the host 2026-10-30. **Proven** means a command showed it that day.
**Planned** means the owner still has to do it.

## What you need to do

1. Finish bringing the trees into the one repo. Leave the clone stopped while
   you do that.
2. Make `etched::hackathon` a real identity. The bridge will not do this.
   `provision_container` stops with: prepare the shared physical seed, the
   private writable leaf, and the container outside the bridge; the bridge
   cannot compose, mount, or copy an identity root. A new public key is
   accepted only when it is already an active registered principal. Register
   public key `Wycws7Udq0XTSN7I45JPP+CL9ZS4MxhXlhM4zAn8FX0=`, then run the
   external seed provision so the sled binds session
   `cc59ab57-d94a-8334-222b-8077ef033320` to Incus instance `etched-hackathon`.
   Do not edit sled or Cozo rows by hand. Do not add a Btrfs member from
   login or start.
3. Prove the binding. A `get_own_identity` call on a mount whose
   `--lungs-session` is `cc59ab57-d94a-8334-222b-8077ef033320` must return that
   session. Until it does, leave `/etc/sv/subsidiary-hackathon-3tchedfs/run`
   on the root session `b0c777e3-0955-cd8b-3d01-ca12998cae28`.
4. After that proof, change `SESSION=` in that run script to the clone
   session and restart `subsidiary-hackathon-3tchedfs`. A call as Linux user
   `3tched` through `/home/3tched/Hackathon/3tchedfs` must then return the
   clone session.
5. Internet on `etched0` is a later step. The bridge is down, fail-mode
   `secure`, with no address and no uplink, so the clone's NIC cannot reach
   3tched and cannot reach the internet. Do not rebuild `etched0` with
   `ovs-vsctl` (the 2026-10-28 correction in
   `docs/src/operations/network.md`). `openflow.write` stays withheld until
   enforcement refuses a flow on any bridge other than `etched0`. Do not put
   the old `hackbr0` NIC back on the root chatbot.

Leave the root chatbot as `3tchedCtlChatbot`, session
`b0c777e3-0955-cd8b-3d01-ca12998cae28`. It is the root, not the subsidiary.

## New

New on 2026-10-30, because the sealed identity path cannot assign the key:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Display name | `etched::hackathon` |
| Incus name | `etched-hackathon` (a name cannot contain `::`) |
| State | Stopped. **Proven.** |
| Session | `cc59ab57-d94a-8334-222b-8077ef033320`, Blake3 `derive_session_id` of the new public key |
| Public key | `Wycws7Udq0XTSN7I45JPP+CL9ZS4MxhXlhM4zAn8FX0=` |
| Private key | `/root/etched-hackathon.key` inside the container, mode 600, root. The host copy was removed. |
| Disk | Its own root volume on pool `3tched`. The root chatbot's persist volume is not attached. |
| Profile | `3tched-lungs`, so a later start can see the lungs socket |
| NIC | `eth0`, bridged, parent `etched0` only. Not `ovsbr0`, not `hackbr0`. |
| Sled | Not registered. This container is not yet an identity. |

The container is a wholesale copy of `3tchedCtlChatbot` with the name and
keys changed. It is not a seed provision and it is not a second root.

## Old and existing

These were already on the host. They were not replaced.

| Item | What it still is |
|---|---|
| Root chatbot | `3tchedCtlChatbot`, running, display name `control-plane-chatbot`, session `b0c777e3-0955-cd8b-3d01-ca12998cae28`, public key `Env5zPMmM1Zhypu5/DY/yU4PRYW/4AOEq2KZ4OSc+18=`, persist volume `3tchedCtlChatbot-persist`. **Proven** still running after the copy. |
| Hackathon mount | `/home/3tched/Hackathon/3tchedfs`, runit `subsidiary-hackathon-3tchedfs`, Linux user `3tched` (uid 1001). **Proven** mounted. `SESSION=` is still the root session. |
| `etched0` | OVS bridge, fail-mode `secure`, no address, no uplink, no extra ports. Created 2026-10-28 with `ovs-vsctl`, so it has no identity and no receipt. |
| `hackbr0` | The 2026-10-28 internet-only Incus bridge. It is down. Its NIC is not on the root container and not on the clone. |
| Other instances | `3tched-container` and `chatbot-template-sysprep` are stopped. `qdrant-recovered` is running. None of them is the subsidiary. |
| Identity rule | The sled is the identity. Session id is derived from the public key. The bridge verifies storage; it does not compose a root. |

The 2026-10-28 docs said the hackathon subsidiary *was* `3tchedCtlChatbot`.
That sentence described the mount that is still live. It is not the owner
model as of 2026-10-30.

## What changed in the old

Brought forward only far enough for the clone to exist beside the root.
Nothing below re-keyed the root or moved the live mount.

| Old thing | Change on 2026-10-30 |
|---|---|
| `3tchedCtlChatbot` | Copied to `etched-hackathon` with `incus copy --instance-only`. The source was left running, on the same session, with the same public key and the same persist volume. |
| Copy's inherited identity labels | Display name, public key, session id, and `lxc.uts.name` set to the clone. `user.opdbus.creation_digest` and `user.opdbus.creation_operation` unset so the copy does not claim the root's creation receipt. |
| Copy's `persist` device | Removed, so the clone does not mount `3tchedCtlChatbot-persist`. |
| `etched0` | The bridge was not edited. The clone's Incus NIC names it as parent. While the clone is stopped, `etched0` still has no extra ports. |
| Hackathon run script and mount | Unchanged. Calls as `3tched` are still the root chatbot. |
| `docs/SUBSIDIARY-SLED.md`, `docs/RUNTIME.md`, `docs/DEV-CYCLE.md` | The old "the subsidiary is the root container" lines now point here. |
| `docs/src/operations/network.md` | A 2026-10-30 note records the clone NIC. The 2026-10-28 `etched0` and `hackbr0` notes stay as history. |

## Also on the host, not the subsidiary

Stale release-kit copies from 2026-10-18 and 2026-10-23 were removed because
their `op-release` binaries did not match the installed kit. The installed
kit that remains is `/usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release/op-release`,
`op-release-launch`, and `/etc/init.d/op-release-activate`, with
`manifest.sha256` matching those three. Slot B
`release-640f40aa-7b7a-446e-a614-3aecb7771d90` was left mounted. The
unfinished journal at `quiescent-delete:489` for candidate
`release-97d42309-3d63-4227-ac48-23f492466652` was left in `slots.json`.
That journal is not this subsidiary.
